questions.question: In a replicated database, a network partition cuts one replica off from the other replicas. If a client asks that replica to read a value, what choice does the replica face?

options.text: Answer from its local copy, which may be stale, or refuse the request and stay consistent
Lose writes already acknowledged, or stop accepting writes until durability is restored
Re-shard its data onto reachable nodes, or replicate the data more widely
Merge its value with the other side by timestamp, keeping the read both current and available

questions.explanation: A disconnected replica cannot know whether the unreachable replicas hold a newer value. If it answers from its local copy, it stays available but may return stale (non-linearizable) data; if it waits or returns an error, it preserves linearizability but becomes unavailable. This is the trade-off that CAP describes. Merging with the other side is impossible precisely because the other side is unreachable, and re-sharding or adding replicas does nothing to resolve the uncertainty about recent writes.

questions.question: What is the simplest, though often unacceptable, way for a distributed service to handle a fault in one of its internal components?

options.text: Let the entire service fail and show the user an error message
Retry every failed request indefinitely until the component recovers
Fail over automatically to a replica chosen by a consensus protocol
Log the fault and keep serving whatever the faulty component returns

questions.explanation: The simplest policy is to give up: let the whole service fail and show an error. When that is unacceptable, the service must be fault-tolerant, meaning it keeps functioning correctly even though some internal component is faulty. Automatic failover via consensus is one of the sophisticated fault-tolerance mechanisms, not the simple option; retrying forever may never finish; and silently serving faulty results is not handling the fault at all.

questions.question: Fault-tolerant algorithms such as consensus for systems in a typical datacenter are designed under certain fault assumptions. Which faults are they usually expected to tolerate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Packets can be lost, reordered, duplicated, or arbitrarily delayed in the network
Clocks are approximate at best
Nodes can pause for a considerable amount of time or crash at any time
Nodes may lie and send arbitrary faulty responses

questions.explanation: The usual datacenter model allows unreliable networks, inaccurate clocks, pauses, and crash failures. It excludes Byzantine nodes that deliberately lie or send contradictory messages, which require stronger protocols.

optionExplanations.a: Network communication is asynchronous and unreliable: a correct algorithm must tolerate loss, duplication, reordering, and unbounded delay without allowing different nodes to decide differently.
optionExplanations.b: Physical clocks can drift or jump, so consensus safety cannot depend on timestamps being perfectly synchronized. Logical terms or epochs are used instead to order leadership and decisions.
optionExplanations.c: A long pause is indistinguishable from slowness or failure to remote nodes, and a node may crash at any point. The protocol must preserve safety while a quorum continues without it.
optionExplanations.d: Arbitrary lying is a Byzantine failure, which is outside the ordinary crash-fault model used for datacenter systems. Tolerating contradictory or malicious messages requires Byzantine-fault-tolerant protocols.

questions.question: A transaction lets an application pretend that certain problems do not exist, even though they do occur. Which illusions does the transaction abstraction provide? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That there are no crashes partway through a set of writes (atomicity)
That nobody else is concurrently accessing the database (isolation)
That storage devices are perfectly reliable (durability)
That every network message is eventually delivered (reliable messaging)

questions.explanation: A good way to build fault-tolerant systems is to find general-purpose abstractions with useful guarantees, implement them once, and let applications rely on them. Transactions are the model: atomicity hides crashes, isolation hides concurrent access, and durability hides storage failures, so the application need not handle those problems itself. Consensus plays the same role for distributed systems. Reliable delivery of every network message is not something transactions promise; a transaction may simply abort if a participant cannot be reached.

optionExplanations.a: Atomicity lets the application act as if a multi-write transaction either happened completely or not at all. Crashes still occur; atomicity hides their partial effects by rolling back incomplete transactions.
optionExplanations.b: Isolation lets each transaction behave as though it were alone in the database. The database enforces that illusion with locking, serial execution, or conflict detection, so race conditions are hidden from the application.
optionExplanations.c: Durability lets the application treat committed data as safe, as if disks never failed. In reality disks do fail; the database hides this with write-ahead logs, replication, and similar techniques.
optionExplanations.d: Transactions do not promise that network messages are eventually delivered. Reliable communication is a separate concern, and a distributed transaction may abort when a participant is unreachable.

questions.question: In distributed systems, what is consensus, and why is it harder than it sounds?

options.text: Getting several nodes to agree on something; hard because nodes crash and messages get lost or delayed
Electing a leader by timeout; hard because every node's timer must be synchronized to one global clock
Replicating every write to all nodes; hard because a disk can fail before the write is flushed
Detecting failed nodes perfectly; hard only because physical clocks drift apart over time

questions.explanation: Informally, consensus means getting several nodes to agree on something, such as who the leader is or whether a transaction commits. That sounds simple, but a node that stays silent may have crashed or may merely be slow or partitioned, and messages may arrive late or not at all; a correct protocol must still make one decision that every node accepts. Leader election is one use of consensus, but naive timeout races can elect two leaders, and no synchronized global clock is assumed. Copying writes to every node is replication, not agreement. Perfect failure detection is impossible with unbounded network delays, so it cannot be the definition either.

questions.question: A database uses single-leader replication and its leader dies. For which task do the remaining nodes typically use consensus?

options.text: Agreeing which node becomes the new leader, so that only one node acts as leader
Deciding which partition each key belongs to after the leader failed
Deciding when to compact the SSTables that the dead leader left behind
Choosing the isolation level for transactions that were in flight

questions.explanation: When failing over, the remaining nodes must agree on exactly one new leader. If two nodes both believe they are leader (split brain), both accept writes, their data diverges, and data is often lost. Consensus prevents this by making all nodes agree on the same choice. Partition assignment, compaction, and isolation levels are unrelated to replacing a failed leader.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how linearizability, ordering of operations, and consensus are related?

options.text: A linearizable store implies a total order of operations, and agreeing on such an order fault-tolerantly is equivalent to consensus
Consensus is a special case of linearizability, and linearizability itself places no constraint at all on the order in which operations occur
Ordering is needed only when consensus is unavailable, acting as a cheaper fallback that replaces linearizability in such systems
The three are independent concerns, and each can be solved on its own without relying on, or implying, either of the other two

questions.explanation: A linearizable register behaves as if there were one copy of the data with every operation taking effect atomically at one point in time, which means all operations fall into a single total order. Getting all nodes to agree on such an order despite faults is total order broadcast, and total order broadcast (like a linearizable compare-and-set register) is provably equivalent to consensus. So the three topics are deeply linked rather than independent, and ordering is the bridge between linearizability and consensus.

questions.question: Why is it worth understanding the fundamental limits (impossibility results) of distributed systems before choosing algorithms?

options.text: Because some faults can be tolerated while the system keeps working, while others make certain guarantees impossible
Because distributed algorithms change so often that the specific algorithms are not worth learning in detail
Because formal proofs are always more useful in practice than working, well-tested implementations of algorithms
Because any algorithm that comes with a correctness proof can then tolerate every possible kind of fault

questions.explanation: In some situations a system can tolerate faults and continue working; in others no algorithm can. Knowing where that boundary lies tells you which guarantee must be weakened under a given failure model, for example that linearizability and availability cannot both hold during a network partition. Without that map, an algorithm may look correct in normal tests while relying on an assumption that breaks during a partition or crash. Proofs only hold under their stated model, so they do not cover every fault.

questions.question: In a replicated database, why might two nodes return different data if you query both at exactly the same moment?

options.text: Because write requests arrive at different nodes at different times
Because of clock skew, a problem that affects only leaderless replication
Because of sharding, a problem that affects only multi-leader replication
Because of network faults, a problem that affects only single-leader replication

questions.explanation: Replication delivers each write to each node over a network with variable delay, so at any instant some nodes have applied a write and others have not. This happens no matter which replication method is used: single-leader, multi-leader, or leaderless. The distractors are wrong because each restricts a universal problem to one replication style.

questions.question: Which statement correctly defines eventual consistency in a replicated database?

options.text: If you stop writing and wait for some unspecified length of time, eventually all reads return the same value
Every read returns the latest write once a bounded, configured replication delay has passed since the write was accepted
All replicas converge on the same value within one second of each write, even while further writes continue arriving
All reads that are served by the same node return the same value, regardless of what other nodes return at that time

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency only promises that if writes stop, replicas eventually converge, assuming network faults are eventually repaired; a better name might be convergence. It says nothing about when that happens: there is no time bound, so options with a fixed delay describe a much stronger guarantee. Consistency among reads on one node is also not what the model is about; it is about all replicas eventually agreeing.

questions.question: Eventual consistency is a very weak guarantee. Which of the following does it NOT promise? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A bound on how long the replicas take to converge
That reads before convergence return a meaningful value rather than anything or nothing
That a client immediately reads back a value it has just written
That replicas converge to the same value once writes stop and faults are repaired

questions.explanation: Eventual consistency promises only convergence: if you stop writing and wait an unspecified time, all replicas end up with the same value. It gives no deadline, it says nothing about what reads return before convergence (they could return anything or nothing), and a read right after your own write may go to a lagging replica and miss it. The one thing it does promise is the eventual convergence itself.

optionExplanations.a: Eventual consistency sets no deadline for convergence. Mistaking it for a bounded-staleness guarantee is a common error that leads applications to assume data will be fresh after some fixed delay.
optionExplanations.b: Before convergence, different replicas may return old values, new values, or nothing at all. The model constrains only the final destination, not the intermediate results that reads observe.
optionExplanations.c: Reading your own writes is a stronger, session-level guarantee. Under bare eventual consistency a client may write through one replica and immediately read an older value from another.
optionExplanations.d: Convergence once writes stop is exactly what eventual consistency does promise, so it is not in the list of things it fails to promise. The weakness is that convergence has no time bound.

questions.question: Why is eventual consistency hard for application developers to work with?

options.text: Unlike a variable in a single-threaded program, a read shortly after a write may return an old value or fail
Its read and write API is unfamiliar compared with the APIs of ordinary single-node databases, so it is harder to learn
It requires the developer to write custom conflict-resolution code for every single write that the application issues
Its behaviour can never be tested in any systematic way, even with deliberate fault injection in a staging environment

questions.explanation: Developers naturally reason as if a database were a variable: assign a value, read it shortly afterward, and get that value back. A database looks like such a variable, but under eventual consistency the read may return an older value or fail, for an unbounded time. The API itself is ordinary, conflict resolution is not always manual, and the behaviour can be tested, though its edge cases appear mainly during faults or high concurrency.

questions.question: Why are bugs caused by relying on weak consistency guarantees hard to find by testing?

options.text: The application usually works; edge cases show up only during faults such as network interruptions, or at high concurrency
Stale reads happen only when clocks are skewed, and test clusters usually have well-synchronized clocks
The anomalies are caused by the database rather than the application, so application tests cannot observe them
Test suites cannot be run against a real replicated database, so consistency behaviour is never exercised during testing

questions.explanation: With weak guarantees such as eventual consistency, replicas are usually close to up to date, so the application behaves correctly in ordinary tests. Anomalies like stale reads show up mainly when there is a fault (for example a network interruption) or under high concurrency, which ordinary tests rarely reproduce. Stale reads come from replication lag, not only from clock skew, and they are visible to the application, so application-level tests with deliberate fault injection can expose them.

questions.question: What is the trade-off when a data system offers stronger consistency guarantees than eventual consistency?

options.text: Possibly worse performance or less fault tolerance, in exchange for being easier to use correctly
Better performance under faults, in exchange for a more complicated programming model
Lower latency for every request, in exchange for needing more replicas to stay correct
Less correctness, in exchange for better performance and higher availability

questions.explanation: Stronger guarantees require more coordination between replicas, so systems that provide them may have worse latency or throughput, or become unavailable during some faults. In return they are easier for application developers to use correctly, because fewer anomalies need handling. The trade-off runs the opposite way from the distractors: strong guarantees cost performance and fault tolerance rather than buying them, and they increase rather than reduce correctness.

questions.question: How do distributed consistency models (such as linearizability) relate to transaction isolation levels (such as serializability)?

options.text: Partly overlapping but mostly independent: isolation prevents races between concurrent transactions, while consistency coordinates replica state despite delays and faults
They are exactly the same hierarchy of guarantees, described under two different names by the transaction-processing and distributed-systems communities
Every isolation level implies one matching distributed consistency model, so choosing an isolation level automatically fixes the consistency model
Consistency models apply only to single-node databases, whereas isolation levels apply only to replicated databases spread across several nodes

questions.explanation: Transaction isolation is primarily about preventing race conditions between concurrently executing transactions. Distributed consistency is mostly about coordinating the state of replicas in the face of delays and faults. They overlap somewhat (strict serializability combines both), but a database can, for example, offer serializable transactions whose reads come from a stale snapshot, so neither guarantee fixes the other.

questions.question: Linearizability makes a replicated system appear as if there were only one copy of the data, with atomic operations. By which other names is it known? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Atomic consistency
Strong consistency
Immediate consistency, or external consistency
Eventual consistency

questions.explanation: Linearizability is also called atomic consistency, strong consistency, immediate consistency, or external consistency. All names describe the same idea: the system behaves as though there is a single, up-to-date copy of the data, so a read always sees the most recent completed write. Eventual consistency is the opposite end of the spectrum, allowing replicas to disagree for an unbounded time.

optionExplanations.a: Atomic consistency is an established name for linearizability. 'Atomic' refers to each operation appearing to take effect at a single instant on the single logical copy.
optionExplanations.b: Strong consistency is a common, if loosely used, name for linearizability. It contrasts with weaker models such as eventual consistency that allow stale reads.
optionExplanations.c: Immediate consistency and external consistency are further names for the same real-time single-copy guarantee. They emphasize that a completed write is visible immediately and agrees with externally observed order.
optionExplanations.d: Eventual consistency allows replicas to disagree temporarily with no bound on staleness, whereas linearizability forbids stale reads. Treating them as synonyms reverses the distinction.

questions.question: Which scenario illustrates a violation of linearizability?

options.text: Alice sees a final score and tells Bob; Bob then reloads, but a lagging replica shows the match still in progress
A read that starts before a write begins and finishes after the write completes returns the old value of the record
Two clients read at exactly the same moment while a write is still in progress, and they get two different values
A read that starts after a write has completed returns the new value, served by a follower rather than by the leader

questions.explanation: Linearizability is a recency guarantee: once an operation has completed and observed a value, any operation that starts later must see that value or a newer one. Bob started his reload after Alice's read completed (he heard her), so returning the older state is a violation. A read that overlaps a write may legally return either the old or the new value, so the second and third scenarios are allowed, and a later read returning the new value is exactly what linearizability requires.

questions.question: Alice and Bob are in the same room. Alice reloads a sports page, sees the final score, and exclaims it. Bob then reloads and is served by a lagging replica that shows the game still in progress. What makes Bob's stale result a linearizability violation rather than acceptable concurrency?

options.text: Bob started his request after Alice's had completed, so his result must be at least as recent as hers
The replica that served Bob was lagging more than one second behind the leader, which exceeds the allowed limit
Bob's request was routed to a different replica from the one that served Alice's request a moment earlier
The final score had already been flushed to disk on the leader before Bob pressed reload on his own phone

questions.explanation: If Alice and Bob had reloaded at the same moment, getting different results would be unsurprising, since neither knows exactly when their request was processed. But Bob knows he initiated his query after Alice's query had returned, so a linearizable system must give him a result at least as recent as hers. What matters is this real-time ordering between the two requests, not how far the replica lagged or which replica served the request.

questions.question: In distributed systems literature, a single value that clients read and write is called a register. What might a register correspond to in a real database?

options.text: One key in a key-value store, one row in a relational table, or one document in a document database
An entire table, an entire secondary index, or an entire partition of the dataset stored on one node
A transaction, a lock, or a lease that a client holds while it reads and writes several values together
A replica node, a physical disk, or a whole file system that stores many independently addressable values

questions.explanation: Linearizability is defined on individual objects called registers. In practice a register could be one key in a key-value store, one row in a relational database, or one document in a document database. It is a single independently addressable value, not a collection such as a table or partition, not a concurrency mechanism such as a lock, and not a piece of infrastructure such as a node or disk.

questions.question: When the timing of client requests to a database is drawn with each request as a horizontal bar along a time axis, what do the start and end of a bar represent?

options.text: The client sending the request, and the client receiving the response
The database starting to process the request, and the write becoming durable
The transaction beginning, and the transaction committing
The request leaving the client, and the request arriving at the database

questions.explanation: Each bar is drawn from the client's point of view: it starts when the client sends the request and ends when the client receives the response. Because network delays vary, the client does not know exactly when the database processed the request, only that it happened somewhere within that interval. Linearizability analysis places each operation's effect at some instant inside its bar; the database's internal processing and durability are not visible to the client.

questions.question: A linearizable register x initially holds 0. Client C writes 1 to x while clients A and B repeatedly read x. Which statements about the values those reads may return are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A read that completes before the write begins must return the old value 0
A read that begins after the write has completed must return the new value 1
A read that overlaps the write in time may return either 0 or 1
A read that overlaps the write must return 1, because the write has already been sent

questions.explanation: A read entirely before the write must see 0, and a read that starts after the write completes must see 1. A read that overlaps the write is concurrent with it, so it may return either value, because we do not know whether the write has taken effect when the read is processed. Linearizability adds one more rule on top of this: once any read has returned 1, later reads must not return 0 again.

optionExplanations.a: A read that completes before the write starts cannot be ordered after that write, so it must return the initial value. Real-time precedence fixes the order of nonoverlapping operations.
optionExplanations.b: A read that starts after the write completes must be ordered after it and therefore see the new value (or a later one). Returning 0 would move the register backward in time.
optionExplanations.c: An overlapping read is concurrent with the write, so its point of effect may fall before or after the write's point of effect. Either value fits a legal single-copy history.
optionExplanations.d: Sending a write does not mean it has already taken effect. During the overlap the read may legally be processed first, so requiring the new value is too strong.

questions.question: In a linearizable register, reads that overlap a write may return either the old or the new value. What additional constraint does linearizability impose on those reads?

options.text: Once any read has returned the new value, every read that starts afterward must also return it
Every read must be served by the leader node rather than by a follower, so that it always sees the newest value
Every write must be replicated synchronously to all replicas before any read is allowed to observe its value
Two reads that are concurrent with each other must always return the same value, whether it is old or new

questions.explanation: If overlapping reads could return old or new values freely, a reader might see the value flip back and forth during a write, which is not how a single copy behaves. (A register with only that weaker rule is called a regular register.) Linearizability requires that there is some instant at which the value atomically flips; after any read has returned the new value, all subsequent reads on any client must return it too, even if the write has not yet completed. The other options describe implementation choices or a rule linearizability does not impose.

questions.question: What does an atomic compare-and-set operation cas(x, v_old, v_new) do?

options.text: Sets x to v_new only if x currently equals v_old; otherwise it leaves x unchanged and returns an error
Adds one to the current value of x and returns the incremented value to the caller in the same atomic step
Reads the current value of x, then writes v_new in a separate later step that other clients may interleave with
Appends v_new to the end of a log of values recorded for x, keeping every earlier value available for reading

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set checks the current value and updates it in one atomic step: if x equals v_old it is set to v_new, otherwise the operation fails and x is unchanged. This lets a client update a value only if nobody else has changed it in the meantime, for example claiming a username only if it is still free. Increment-and-get and log append are different atomic operations, and a non-atomic read followed by a write allows exactly the race that compare-and-set prevents.

questions.question: When checking whether a history of operations on a register is linearizable, at what point is each operation considered to take effect?

options.text: At one instant between sending the request and receiving its response, with those instants never going back in time
At the instant the client sends the request, with the points allowed to move backward in time whenever this is needed
At the instant the write becomes durable on disk at the leader, with no constraint at all on the order of those points
At the instant the request arrives at the first replica over the network, ordered strictly by those arrival times

questions.explanation: Each operation is imagined to execute atomically at some instant within its request-response interval. Joining these instants in sequence must give a valid register history (each read returns the most recent write) and must always move forward in time. That forward-only requirement is what gives the recency guarantee: once a value has been written or read, all later reads see it until it is overwritten. Send time, durability, and arrival time are not the reference points.

questions.question: Three requests to a linearizable register x are concurrent: client B sends a read, then client D sends write x = 0, then client A sends write x = 1. B's read returns 1. Why is this still linearizable?

options.text: The requests are concurrent, so the database may process D's write, then A's write, then B's read
Reads are always served directly from the leader, which by then already holds the newest value of x
A read that is sent before any write is permitted to return any value at all, so 1 is as good as 0
B's read carried a later timestamp than both of the writes, so it had to return the most recent value

questions.explanation: Linearizability constrains only operations that do not overlap in time. Since all three requests overlap, the database may execute them in any order that forms a valid sequential history, such as D's write, then A's write, then B's read. That order differs from the send order, which is fine; perhaps B's request was delayed in the network. A read cannot return 'any value', though: it must return the value of the most recent write in the chosen order.

questions.question: In a linearizable register, client B's read returns 1 before client A has received the 'ok' response for its write of 1. Why is this not a violation?

options.text: The write took effect before B's read; A's ok response was merely delayed in the network
Reads and writes on the same register are independent, so they need not be ordered
B read from a different replica than the one A wrote to, so no ordering applies
It is a violation, because a value must not be visible before the writer has its acknowledgment

questions.explanation: A client knows only that its write took effect somewhere between sending the request and receiving the response. The database may have applied A's write, then served B's read, while the 'ok' to A was still travelling. This does not mean the value was read before it was written. Reads and writes on one register must be consistently ordered, and the replica layout is irrelevant to the client-visible definition.

questions.question: On a linearizable register x, client D issues cas(x, 0, 3). By the time the database processes it, another client has already changed x from 0 to 2. What happens to D's operation, and why?

options.text: It fails and leaves x unchanged, because x no longer equals the expected value 0
It succeeds, because D sent its request before the other client's write
It succeeds but is applied after the other write, overwriting 2 with 3
It blocks until x becomes 0 again and then succeeds

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set succeeds only if the register holds the expected value at the instant the operation takes effect. Linearizability gives no isolation from other clients, so x may change at any time; cas is precisely the tool for detecting that. Because x is 2 rather than 0 when D's cas is processed, the operation returns an error and leaves x unchanged. Send order does not matter, and cas neither overwrites unconditionally nor waits.

questions.question: On a linearizable register, client C's cas changes x from 2 to 4. While that cas is in progress, client A reads 4. After A's read has completed, client B starts a read that returns 2. Is this history linearizable?

options.text: No: B's read started after A had already read 4, so B may not return an older value
Yes: B's read overlaps C's cas, so it may return either 2 or 4
Yes: linearizability constrains only writes, not the values that reads return
No: A's read is the violation, because it returned 4 before C's cas completed

questions.explanation: Considered alone, B's read overlaps C's cas, so returning 2 would be fine. But A has already read the new value 4 and completed before B started, and once any read has seen a new value, later reads must not see an older one. A's read is legal because a read may observe a concurrent write before that write's response arrives. Checking linearizability like this is possible but computationally expensive: record the timings of all requests and responses and test whether some valid sequential order fits them.

questions.question: What does serializability guarantee?

options.text: Transactions, each possibly reading and writing multiple objects, behave as if executed in some serial order
Every read of a single register returns the most recent completed write in real time
Transactions execute in an order that matches the real-time order in which they started
Single-object operations are atomic, but multi-object transactions are not covered

questions.explanation: Serializability is an isolation property of transactions, where each transaction may read and write several objects. It guarantees the result is the same as if transactions had run one at a time in some serial order, and that order may differ from the order in which they actually ran. The real-time recency guarantee on a single object is linearizability, which is a different property.

questions.question: Which statement about linearizability is correct?

options.text: It is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of an individual object, and alone it does not prevent write skew
It groups related operations into transactions, and therefore it prevents anomalies such as write skew automatically
It allows reads to return stale values for a while, as long as all of the replicas eventually converge on one value
It guarantees that transactions touching several objects appear to execute one at a time in some serial order

questions.explanation: Linearizability concerns a single register: every read sees the latest completed write. It does not group operations into transactions, so anomalies such as write skew, which involve a transaction reading some objects and writing others, are not prevented unless extra measures such as materializing conflicts are used. Stale reads are exactly what it forbids, and serial ordering of multi-object transactions is serializability.

questions.question: What is a database called that provides both serializability and linearizability?

options.text: Strict serializability, or strong one-copy serializability
Strong eventual consistency with convergent replicated data types
Snapshot serializability provided by multi-version concurrency control
Atomic broadcast serializability provided by two-phase commit

questions.explanation: The combination of serializable transactions and linearizable (real-time recent) operations is called strict serializability, or strong one-copy serializability (strong-1SR). Serializability implementations based on two-phase locking or actual serial execution are typically linearizable as well, whereas serializable snapshot isolation is not, because it reads from a snapshot. Strong eventual consistency is a weak convergence property, not this combination.

questions.question: Which implementation of serializability is not linearizable, and why?

options.text: Serializable snapshot isolation, because its reads come from a snapshot that excludes writes newer than the snapshot
Two-phase locking, because it releases each transaction's locks before the transaction has finished committing
Actual serial execution, because running every transaction on a single thread causes reads to lose their recency
None of them, because every implementation of serializability is automatically linearizable as well, by definition

questions.explanation: Serializable snapshot isolation deliberately reads from a consistent snapshot so that readers and writers do not contend for locks. The whole point of a snapshot is that it does not include writes more recent than the snapshot, so reads from it can be stale and are not linearizable. Two-phase locking holds locks until commit, and serial execution on one thread processes operations in real-time order; both are typically linearizable.

questions.question: Linearizability and serializability are often confused. Which properties describe linearizability rather than serializability? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is a recency guarantee
It concerns a single object or register
It is an isolation property of transactions spanning multiple objects
Its serial order may differ from the real execution order

questions.explanation: Linearizability concerns real-time recency for one object, while serializability concerns isolation across a transaction's objects. Their similar sequential-language names hide two independent guarantees.

optionExplanations.a: Linearizability is specifically a real-time recency guarantee: once a write completes, later operations must observe it or something newer. Serializability alone does not impose that wall-clock order.
optionExplanations.b: The base definition of linearizability applies independently to a register or object and composes across objects. Serializability instead constrains whole multi-object transactions.
optionExplanations.c: Multi-object transactional isolation is the subject of serializability, not the defining scope of linearizability. Combining both properties yields strict serializability.
optionExplanations.d: A serializable execution may choose a serial order different from real-time order. That flexibility belongs to serializability and is precisely what linearizability removes for nonoverlapping operations.

questions.question: In a system using single-leader replication, how can a lock be used to elect the leader, and what property must the lock have?

options.text: Every node tries to acquire the lock and the winner leads; the lock must be linearizable so all nodes agree who holds it
The node with the lowest ID becomes leader without any lock; an eventually consistent membership list is enough
Every node acquires its own local lock and leads its own partition; the lock need only be local to each node
Every node tries to acquire the lock and the winner leads; an eventually consistent lock is enough because conflicts merge later

questions.explanation: Lock-based leader election works by having every node try to acquire one shared lock at startup; whichever succeeds is leader. However it is implemented, the lock must be linearizable: all nodes must agree on who owns it, otherwise two nodes could each believe they hold it and both act as leader (split brain). An eventually consistent lock is useless for this, because leadership actions cannot be merged afterward.

questions.question: Which coordination services are commonly used to implement distributed locks and leader election, because they implement linearizable operations fault-tolerantly using consensus?

options.text: Apache ZooKeeper and etcd
Memcached and Varnish caching layers
Graphite and Prometheus metrics stores
RabbitMQ and ActiveMQ message brokers

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper and etcd use consensus algorithms to provide linearizable operations that survive node failures, which makes them suitable for locks and leader election. Strictly, their writes are linearizable but reads may be stale by default; a linearizable read needs a quorum read in etcd or sync() in ZooKeeper. Libraries such as Apache Curator add higher-level recipes on top. Caches, metrics stores, and message brokers do not offer fault-tolerant linearizable compare-and-set operations, so they are not a sound basis for locks.

questions.question: How does Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) use distributed locking?

options.text: A linearizable lock per disk page, with nodes sharing one disk storage system over a dedicated interconnect
A lock per table, which nodes acquire by sending messages to each other over the ordinary public network
A lock per transaction, with each node owning separate disks so that no storage is shared between the nodes
No locks at all; it relies only on multi-version concurrency control so that readers never block any writers

questions.explanation: Oracle RAC uses very fine-grained distributed locks: one lock per disk page, with multiple nodes sharing access to the same disk storage system. Because these linearizable locks sit on the critical path of every transaction, RAC deployments usually have a dedicated cluster interconnect network for communication between database nodes. This shows distributed locking applied at a far finer granularity than leader election.

questions.question: Which of these constraints requires linearizability if it must be enforced at the moment data is written?

options.text: No two users may register the same username or email address
Every order row must reference an existing customer row (a foreign key)
Every product's price must be a positive number (an attribute check)
An order's total must equal the sum of its line items, recomputed later

questions.explanation: A hard uniqueness constraint, such as unique usernames or file paths, requires all nodes to agree on a single up-to-date answer so that if two people concurrently claim the same name, exactly one gets an error. That needs linearizability. Foreign key and attribute constraints can be implemented without linearizability, and a derived total that is recomputed later does not require an immediate global decision at all.

questions.question: Registering a unique username in a distributed database is best understood as which kind of operation?

options.text: Acquiring a lock on that name, like a compare-and-set from unclaimed to the new user's ID
Adding a foreign key reference from the accounts table to a separate table of reserved usernames
Merging the divergent replica values afterward using last-write-wins conflict resolution
Running a read-only query first that checks whether the username already exists anywhere

questions.explanation: Claiming a username is like acquiring a lock on that name, or like a compare-and-set that sets the username's owner to your user ID provided it is not already taken. Exactly one concurrent claimant must win. Last-write-wins would silently discard one user's claim after both were told they succeeded, and a separate existence check followed by an insert has a race: another claim can slip in between the check and the write.

questions.question: Which of the following constraints, if enforced strictly, require a single up-to-date value that all nodes agree on? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A bank account balance must never go negative
You must not sell more items than you have in stock in the warehouse
Two people must not concurrently book the same seat on a flight or in a theater
Every row that references another table must point to an existing row (a foreign key)

questions.explanation: Each of the first three constraints depends on one current value, the account balance, the stock level, or the seat occupancy, that every node must agree on before accepting a conflicting operation. Otherwise two nodes could each approve a debit, a sale, or a booking based on stale data. Foreign key constraints, by contrast, can be implemented without linearizability. In practice the first three are sometimes treated loosely, with violations fixed afterward.

optionExplanations.a: Preventing overdrafts requires every competing debit to be checked against one authoritative balance. Two replicas with stale balances could each approve a debit and together drive the balance negative.
optionExplanations.b: Selling stock safely means several buyers must not consume the same remaining unit. Conflicting sales have to be decided against one agreed stock level.
optionExplanations.c: Seat booking is a uniqueness decision: concurrent claims for one seat need exactly one winner, which requires one agreed occupancy value.
optionExplanations.d: Foreign key constraints can be enforced without linearizability, because they do not require all nodes to agree on one current scalar value at the moment of writing.

questions.question: When can an application acceptably enforce a constraint such as 'no overbooked flights' loosely, without linearizability?

options.text: When a violation can be fixed afterward, for example by rebooking customers and compensating them
When the constraint concerns bank balances, since overdrafts are too rare to be worth preventing
When the constraint is a hard uniqueness constraint, such as allowing only one account per username
Never, because every constraint must always be enforced linearizably at the moment the data is written

questions.explanation: Some constraints can be treated loosely when an occasional violation can be repaired: an overbooked flight can be handled by rebooking customers and offering compensation. In such cases linearizability may not be needed. A hard uniqueness constraint, such as those typically found in relational databases, still requires linearizability, and it is not true that every constraint must be enforced that way.

questions.question: Alice sees a final football score on her phone and exclaims it; Bob then reloads and a lagging replica shows the match still in progress. If Alice had said nothing, what would most likely have happened?

options.text: Bob would not have known his result was stale, and a later reload would have shown the score
The database would have detected the stale read itself and reported the staleness to Bob's phone
Bob's first reload would then have been guaranteed to show the final score from an up-to-date replica
The lagging replica would have blocked Bob's read until it had caught up with the leader's latest data

questions.explanation: Bob only noticed the violation because there was an additional communication channel outside the database: Alice's voice reaching Bob's ears. Without it he would have refreshed again a few seconds later and eventually seen the score, never knowing the first result was stale. The database does not detect or report such staleness, and a lagging replica serves the read rather than blocking it.

questions.question: A website lets users upload photos, and a background process creates lower-resolution thumbnails. How are the full-size photo and the resize instruction passed from the web server to the resizer?

options.text: The photo is written to a file storage service, then a small resize instruction is placed on a message queue
The whole photo is placed on the message queue, since brokers handle multi-megabyte messages well
The photo is written to the resizer's local disk, and the resizer polls that directory for new files
The web server calls the resizer synchronously with the photo and waits for the thumbnail

questions.explanation: Most message brokers are designed for small messages, while a photo may be several megabytes. So the web server first writes the photo to a file storage service and, once that write completes, puts a small instruction on the queue telling the resizer to process it. This creates two separate communication channels between the web server and the resizer: the storage service and the queue.

questions.question: A web server writes an uploaded photo to replicated file storage and then places a resize instruction on a message queue. If the file storage is not linearizable, what race can occur?

options.text: The queue message may reach the resizer before storage has replicated the photo, so it reads an old version or nothing
The queue message is always lost when storage is not linearizable, so the photo is never resized and no thumbnail exists
The photo is resized twice because the queue redelivers the job, which wastes capacity but leaves the results consistent
The resizer reads a half-written file because the storage service's write itself was not atomic on any single replica

questions.explanation: The message queue may be faster than the storage service's internal replication. When the resizer fetches the image, it may hit a replica that does not yet have the new version and see an old image or nothing at all. If it resizes an old version, the full-size and resized images in storage become permanently inconsistent, which is worse than a stale sports score on a web page, which corrects itself on the next reload.

questions.question: A web server writes a photo to file storage and then sends a resize job through a message queue. What is the underlying cause of the resulting race, and what is the simplest remedy?

options.text: Two communication channels with no shared ordering; linearizable file storage is the simplest remedy
A message queue that is too slow; switching to a faster message broker removes the race entirely
Storage that is not durable enough; adding more storage replicas removes the race between the channels
A stateless resizer; making the resizer keep state between jobs lets it detect and avoid the race itself

questions.explanation: The race exists because information flows from the web server to the resizer over two channels, file storage and the queue, and without a recency guarantee one can overtake the other. Linearizable storage closes the gap and is the simplest to understand. If you control the extra channel (as with the queue), alternatives similar to read-your-writes techniques also work, for example passing a version identifier through the queue, at the cost of more complexity. A faster queue or more replicas would make the race worse or leave it unchanged.

questions.question: What does linearizability require a replicated datastore to behave like?

options.text: As though there were a single copy of the data, with all operations on it atomic
As though every replica accepted writes independently and merged them later
As though reads lagged writes by at most a bounded, configured delay
As though every operation were part of a multi-object serializable transaction

questions.explanation: Linearizability means 'behave as though there is only a single copy of the data, and all operations on it are atomic.' The simplest implementation would be to really keep only one copy, but that is not fault-tolerant: if the node holding it fails, the data is lost or inaccessible. So real systems replicate, and the question becomes which replication methods can preserve the single-copy illusion. Independent writes with merging and bounded staleness are weaker models, and serializable transactions are a different guarantee.

questions.question: Why is single-leader replication described as only potentially linearizable?

options.text: Leader or synchronous-follower reads can be linearizable, but snapshot isolation, bugs, or a false leader break it
Under heavy load the leader lags behind its own followers, so the reads that the leader serves become stale
Followers apply the log in a different order from the leader, so one read returns different values on each
Linearizable reads must always be sent to asynchronously updated followers, and never to the leader itself

questions.explanation: In single-leader replication the leader holds the primary copy used for writes. Reads from the leader, or from synchronously updated followers, have the potential to be linearizable. But not every single-leader database actually is: some use snapshot isolation by design, some have concurrency bugs, and a node that wrongly believes it is still leader can serve stale data. With asynchronous replication, failover may even lose committed writes. The leader never lags its own followers, followers apply the replication log in the leader's order, and asynchronous followers are exactly the replicas that may be stale.

questions.question: Serving linearizable reads from the leader in single-leader replication rests on what assumption, and how can it fail?

options.text: That you know for sure which node is the leader; a node wrongly believing it still leads may serve stale data
That all node clocks are synchronized; NTP drift between nodes makes the reads served by the leader stale
That quorum sizes stay fixed; rebalancing partitions changes the quorums and makes the leader's reads stale
That the leader's disk never fails; any later disk crash retroactively invalidates all of the earlier reads

questions.explanation: Reading from the leader works only if you know for certain who the leader is. A node may think it is leader when the rest of the cluster has already elected another; if this delusional leader keeps serving requests, it is likely to violate linearizability. Separately, with asynchronous replication a failover may lose committed writes, violating both durability and linearizability. Clock synchronization and quorum sizes are not what leader-based reads depend on.

questions.question: Some consensus algorithms resemble single-leader replication. Why can they implement linearizable storage safely where plain single-leader replication may not?

options.text: They contain measures that prevent split brain and stale replicas
They replicate every write synchronously to all nodes in the cluster
They rely on tightly synchronized clocks between all the nodes
They avoid having any leader node at all

questions.explanation: Consensus protocols such as those behind ZooKeeper and etcd have a leader, but they also include mechanisms (epoch numbers and quorum votes) that prevent two nodes from acting as leader and prevent a stale replica from serving outdated state. Thanks to these details they can implement linearizable storage safely. They need only a majority, not every node, and they do not depend on synchronized clocks.

questions.question: Why are systems with multi-leader replication generally not linearizable?

options.text: They accept writes concurrently on several nodes and replicate them asynchronously, causing conflicts
Their leaders are elected by a consensus algorithm, which is too slow to be linearizable
They replicate writes synchronously across datacenters, which reorders the writes
Their reads are always served by followers rather than by any of the leaders, so reads miss recent writes

questions.explanation: With multi-leader replication, several nodes accept writes at the same time and replicate them to each other asynchronously. Two leaders can therefore accept conflicting writes that later need resolution. Such conflicts are an artifact of not having a single copy of the data, which is exactly what linearizability pretends exists. Multi-leader systems do not elect leaders by consensus, and they replicate asynchronously, not synchronously.

questions.question: Dynamo-style leaderless systems are sometimes claimed to give strong consistency with quorums. Which of the following undermine linearizability in such systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Last-write-wins conflict resolution based on time-of-day clocks
Sloppy quorums with hinted handoff
Variable network delays, even with strict quorums where w + r is greater than n
Read repair, which always restores linearizability by the time the next read is served

questions.explanation: Quorum overlap alone does not create one real-time order. Last-write-wins based on time-of-day clocks (as in Cassandra) is almost certainly nonlinearizable because clock skew means timestamps need not match actual event order. Sloppy quorums ruin any chance of linearizability. Even strict quorums can behave nonlinearizably when a write reaches replicas at different times. It is safest to assume a Dynamo-style system is not linearizable.

optionExplanations.a: Wall-clock last-write-wins can order a causally later write below an earlier one when clocks are skewed. A timestamp comparison therefore cannot guarantee the real-time order that linearizability requires.
optionExplanations.b: Sloppy quorums may accept writes on substitute nodes outside the key's usual replica set, so read and write quorums need not intersect. Quorum counts then provide no current single-copy view.
optionExplanations.c: Even with intersecting strict quorums, a write may reach replicas at different times, so one reader sees the new value and a later reader sees the old one. Intersection is necessary but not sufficient.
optionExplanations.d: Read repair as normally implemented happens asynchronously and helps replicas converge; it does not by itself establish a single real-time order. Only synchronous read repair plus extra writer coordination can make reads and writes linearizable.

questions.question: In a Dynamo-style system with n = 3, a writer sends x = 1 to all three replicas (w = 3). While the write is in progress, client A reads from two replicas (r = 2) and sees 1 on one of them. After A's read completes, client B reads from a different two replicas and gets 0 from both. The quorum condition w + r greater than n holds. Why is this not linearizable?

options.text: B's read began after A's completed yet returned the older value, because the write reached replicas at different times
The quorum condition was in fact violated by the readers' choice of replicas, and that alone explains the anomaly
Both clients eventually read the same value once read repair ran, so there is in fact no anomaly to be explained
The writer reached only two of the three replicas, so the read and write quorums did not overlap as they should

questions.explanation: The write is still propagating: one replica already has 1, while the others still have 0. A's quorum happens to include the updated replica; B's quorum, chosen later, contains two replicas that have not received the write yet. Since B's request starts after A's completes, linearizability would require B to see 1 as well: a later reader may never see an older value than an earlier reader already saw. The quorum condition holds and the writer targets all three replicas; the problem is timing, not quorum arithmetic.

questions.question: What must a Dynamo-style system do to make strict quorum reads and writes linearizable, and at what cost?

options.text: Readers repair stale replicas synchronously before returning, and writers first read a quorum's latest state, costing performance
Nothing extra is needed: strict quorums with w + r greater than n are already linearizable, so there is no added cost at all
Use only asynchronous read repair in the background, which adds no latency to reads or writes and keeps the replicas current
Use last-write-wins conflict resolution with time-of-day clocks, which is linearizable whenever the clocks are synchronized

questions.explanation: Dynamo-style quorums can be made linearizable at a performance cost: a reader must complete read repair synchronously before returning results, and a writer must read the latest state of a quorum before sending its writes. At the time of writing, Riak skipped synchronous read repair because of the performance penalty, and Cassandra waited for read repair on quorum reads but still lost linearizability under concurrent writes to the same key because of last-write-wins. Plain strict quorums are not enough, as concurrent-read races show.

questions.question: Synchronous read repair plus a quorum read before each write can make Dynamo-style reads and writes linearizable. Which operation still cannot be implemented this way?

options.text: Compare-and-set, because choosing one winner among concurrent updates requires consensus
Read, because a linearizable read in a leaderless system always requires a consensus algorithm
Write, because a linearizable write always requires a single leader to order the writes
No operation: compare-and-set can also be made linearizable using these quorum techniques

questions.explanation: These quorum techniques make plain reads and writes linearizable, but a linearizable compare-and-set cannot be built this way: it must pick exactly one winner among concurrent conditional updates, and that decision requires a consensus algorithm. Reads and writes, in contrast, can be made linearizable without consensus in the same system model.

questions.question: Two datacenters each hold replicas of a database, and the network link between them fails while clients can still reach their own datacenter. With multi-leader replication, what happens?

options.text: Each datacenter keeps accepting reads and writes; writes are queued and exchanged once the link returns
Both datacenters become unavailable for writes until the link is restored, though stale reads still work
One datacenter is elected leader by majority vote and the other becomes read-only for the duration
All writes are rejected in both datacenters, but linearizable reads continue to be served in both of them

questions.explanation: With multi-leader replication each datacenter has its own leader and replicates to the other asynchronously. During the interruption both continue operating normally; the writes destined for the other side are queued and exchanged when connectivity returns. The price is that the system is not linearizable: the two sides can diverge and produce conflicts. No election takes place, and writes are not rejected.

questions.question: A database uses single-leader replication across two datacenters, and the link between them fails. Which clients can still perform writes and linearizable reads?

options.text: Only clients that can reach the datacenter containing the leader
Clients in both datacenters, since followers accept writes during the outage
Clients in the follower datacenter, after it is automatically promoted
Clients in neither datacenter, since both datacenters become unavailable for reads and writes during the outage

questions.explanation: All writes and linearizable reads must go to the leader. Clients that can reach the leader's datacenter continue normally. Clients connected only to the follower datacenter cannot write or make linearizable reads until the link is repaired; they can still read from the follower, but those reads might be stale. So for applications that need linearizability, the follower side suffers an outage.

questions.question: If an application requires linearizability and some replicas are disconnected from the others by a network fault, what must those disconnected replicas do?

options.text: Wait until the network is fixed or return an error, and so become unavailable
Keep processing requests independently and reconcile once the network recovers
Serve reads from their local copy but reject writes, which keeps them linearizable
Switch to synchronous replication, which avoids the trade-off entirely

questions.explanation: Any linearizable database faces this, however it is implemented and even within one datacenter. Disconnected replicas cannot know about writes on the other side, so to preserve linearizability they must wait or return an error; either way they are unavailable. Processing requests independently keeps them available but gives up linearizability, and serving local reads while rejecting writes is not enough either, because those reads may miss writes accepted on the other side. Synchronous replication does not help, because it cannot complete across a broken link.

questions.question: Who named the CAP theorem, and how old is the trade-off it describes?

options.text: Eric Brewer named it in 2000, but designers had known the trade-off since the 1970s
Gilbert and Lynch named it in 2000, and the trade-off had been unknown before then
Eric Brewer named it in 1990, and it had already been formally proved back in 1970
Edgar Codd introduced it in 1970, in his paper describing the relational data model

questions.explanation: The CAP theorem was named by Eric Brewer in 2000. The underlying insight, that applications not requiring linearizability can be more tolerant of network problems, had been known to designers of distributed databases since the 1970s. Gilbert and Lynch later gave a formal proof (published in 2002); they did not coin the name.

questions.question: What was CAP originally proposed as, and what lasting influence did it have?

options.text: A rule of thumb without precise definitions, which encouraged engineers to explore shared-nothing designs
A formal theorem with precise definitions from the start, which settled the design debate for distributed databases
A benchmark suite for comparing database products' availability under failure, used by vendors to rank systems
A rule of thumb that, in practice, had no noticeable influence at all on how distributed databases were designed

questions.explanation: CAP began as a rule of thumb, without precise definitions, meant to start a discussion about trade-offs. At the time many distributed databases provided linearizable semantics on clusters with shared storage, and CAP encouraged engineers to explore distributed shared-nothing systems better suited to large web services. It deserves credit for that culture shift, visible in the explosion of NoSQL databases from the mid-2000s, even though its formal version is narrow.

questions.question: Why is it misleading to present CAP as choosing any two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance?

options.text: Network partitions are faults that happen regardless, so partition tolerance is not optional
All three properties can in fact be provided at once, even while a network partition is in progress
Consistency and availability turn out to mean exactly the same thing in CAP's formal definitions
Partition tolerance refers to sharding the data, which any system can simply choose not to do

questions.explanation: Network partitions are faults; they happen whether you like it or not, so 'giving up partition tolerance' is not a real option. The real choice arises only when a partition occurs: stay linearizable or stay available. Note that the P in CAP means a network partition (nodes alive but unable to communicate), not deliberate sharding of data.

questions.question: What is a more accurate way to phrase the CAP trade-off?

options.text: Either consistent or available when partitioned: a healthy network allows both, and a partition forces a choice
Pick any two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance once, at design time, and keep them for good
Always choose availability, since network partitions are too rare in practice to matter for real applications
Always choose consistency, since a network partition makes availability impossible to provide in any case

questions.explanation: When the network works correctly, a system can provide both linearizability and total availability. Only when a network fault occurs must it choose between them, so a better phrasing is 'either Consistent or Available when Partitioned'. A more reliable network makes this choice necessary less often, but eventually the choice is inevitable. Neither blanket rule is right for every application.

questions.question: Why is the term 'availability' problematic in CAP discussions?

options.text: It has several contradictory definitions, and CAP's formal definition does not match its usual meaning
Availability cannot be measured in any meaningful way, even in principle, so the word has no fixed content
In CAP, availability means exactly the same thing as durability, which surprises most of the people using it
In CAP, availability is defined so that it requires linearizability, so the two properties cannot be separated

questions.explanation: Discussions of CAP use several contradictory definitions of availability, and the formal theorem's definition differs from what engineers usually mean by the word. Many systems marketed as highly available (fault-tolerant) do not meet CAP's idiosyncratic definition. This confusion is one reason CAP is best avoided as a way of describing systems. Availability is measurable, is distinct from durability, and is in tension with linearizability rather than requiring it.

questions.question: What is the scope of the CAP theorem as formally defined?

options.text: Narrow: one consistency model (linearizability) and one kind of fault (network partitions)
Broad: every consistency model and every kind of fault, including network delays
The trade-off between latency and throughput in a loaded system
Byzantine faults as well as network partitions between honest nodes

questions.explanation: The formal CAP theorem considers only linearizability and only network partitions, meaning nodes that are alive but disconnected from each other. It says nothing about network delays, dead nodes, or other trade-offs such as latency. Because of this narrow scope it has little practical value for designing systems, despite its historical influence.

questions.question: How useful is the CAP theorem for designing distributed systems today?

options.text: Of little practical value; superseded by more precise results, it is mostly of historical interest
It remains the primary design framework that every distributed system should be built around today
It has been proved false by later research, so its conclusions should simply be ignored by designers
It is useful only for NoSQL databases, where it fully describes every trade-off that designers face

questions.explanation: CAP was historically influential, but because it covers only one consistency model and one fault, it says little about normal-case latency, other consistency models, or other faults. It has been superseded by more precise impossibility results, so it is mostly of historical interest. It is not false; it is just too narrow to guide design decisions.

questions.question: Which of the following is a surprising example of a system that is not linearizable?

options.text: RAM on a modern multi-core CPU, unless memory barriers or fences are used
A single-node database executing transactions serially on one thread
An in-process key-value store holding one copy of each key, accessed under a lock
A register implemented on top of a consensus algorithm such as Raft

questions.explanation: On a multi-core CPU, a thread on one core writing a memory address and a thread on another core reading it shortly afterward is not guaranteed to see the new value unless a memory barrier or fence is used. Each core has its own cache and store buffer, and changes are written to main memory asynchronously, so there are several copies of the data updated asynchronously. The other options all keep a single copy or use consensus, which makes them linearizable.

questions.question: Multi-core CPUs drop linearizability for memory access. Why is it wrong to justify this with the CAP theorem?

options.text: Communication within one computer is assumed reliable; linearizability is dropped for performance, not fault tolerance
Because CAP applies only to databases and networked services, and it can never be applied to any kind of hardware
Because CPU caches are in fact always linearizable, so nothing is actually dropped and there is nothing to justify
Because a disconnected core is expected to keep running normally, so partitions inside the CPU are already tolerated

questions.explanation: Within one computer we assume reliable communication, and we do not expect a CPU core to keep operating normally if it is disconnected from the rest of the machine. So the multi-core memory model has nothing to do with partitions; it drops linearizability because caches make memory access much faster. Many distributed databases that avoid linearizability do so for the same reason: linearizability is slow all the time, not only during a network fault.

questions.question: What did Attiya and Welch prove about the performance of linearizability, and what follows?

options.text: Response time is at least proportional to the uncertainty of network delays, so it is high on networks with variable delay
Linearizability is impossible to implement at all in an asynchronous network, so every claim to provide it is false
Linearizability always costs exactly a constant factor of two in latency, regardless of how variable the network is
Linearizability is free whenever the network is reliable, so its cost can safely be ignored in a single datacenter

questions.explanation: Attiya and Welch proved that if you want linearizability, the response time of reads and writes is at least proportional to the uncertainty of delays in the network. Most computer networks have highly variable delays, so linearizable operations inevitably have high response times; no faster algorithm exists. Weaker consistency models can be much faster, which is why the trade-off matters for latency-sensitive systems.

questions.question: Why does the definition of a linearizable register imply that its operations have a well-defined order?

options.text: Each operation appears to take effect atomically at one instant on a single copy, so those instants form one sequence
Because linearizability requires synchronized physical clocks, which attach a timestamp to every single operation
Because linearizability requires a single leader node, which assigns a sequence number to every single operation
It does not imply any order, because linearizability constrains only the values that reads return, never their order

questions.explanation: A linearizable register behaves as if there is a single copy of the data and every operation takes effect atomically at one instant. Placing those instants on a timeline gives one sequence: for any two operations you can say which happened first. That total order is what links linearizability to ordering and, ultimately, to consensus. Linearizability can be implemented without synchronized clocks, and it is defined independently of any leader.

questions.question: Ordering of operations is a recurring concern in data systems. In which of the following does establishing an order play a central role? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Single-leader replication, where the leader fixes the order of writes in the replication log
Serializability, where transactions behave as if executed one at a time in some serial order
Timestamps and clocks, used to decide which of two writes happened later
The sorted order of keys in a B-tree page, which decides which of two concurrent writes happened first

questions.explanation: The main purpose of a leader in single-leader replication is to determine the order in which followers apply writes. Serializability is about transactions behaving as if executed in some sequential order. Timestamps and clocks are another attempt to impose order, for example to decide which of two writes happened later. Ordering connects these features, and it is also deeply linked to linearizability and consensus.

optionExplanations.a: A single leader serializes accepted writes into one replication-log order that followers replay. Without a single leader, concurrent writes can conflict.
optionExplanations.b: Serializability is defined by equivalence to some one-at-a-time transaction order, achieved by literally serial execution or by preventing serialization conflicts with locking or aborts.
optionExplanations.c: Timestamps and clocks try to establish whether one operation came before another, as in last-write-wins conflict resolution. Their limitations appear when clock order diverges from real order.
optionExplanations.d: Key ordering within a B-tree page determines storage layout and lookup, not the temporal order of operations. Which of two concurrent writes happened first is unrelated to where their keys sort.

questions.question: In a replicated chat, an observer sees an answer to a question before seeing the question itself. Which guarantee is violated, and what relationship links the two messages?

options.text: Consistent prefix reads; the answer is causally dependent on the question
Read-your-writes; the two messages are concurrent with each other
Monotonic reads; the two messages have no causal relationship
Durability; the question was lost and later restored from a backup

questions.explanation: The person answering must have seen the question, so the answer causally depends on it: the question has to come first. Seeing the answer without its question violates consistent prefix reads, a guarantee that readers see writes in an order that respects causality. The messages are not concurrent (one caused the other), and nothing was lost.

questions.question: In multi-leader replication with three leaders, an update to a row reaches one replica before the insert that created the row, so the replica sees an update to a row that does not exist. Which causal rule is violated?

options.text: A row must be created before it can be updated
Two leaders must never write to the same row
A leader must never lose a write during failover
A follower must never lag behind its leader

questions.explanation: Network delays let some writes overtake others between leaders. Causality here means the row's creation must happen before its update, because the update depends on the row existing. A replica that receives the update first appears to update a nonexistent row. Leaders writing the same row, lost writes on failover, and follower lag are different problems.

questions.question: For any two operations A and B in a distributed system, what are the possible relationships under the happens-before relation?

options.text: A happened before B, B happened before A, or A and B are concurrent
A happened before B or B happened before A; concurrency cannot occur
A and B either conflict with each other or do not conflict
A and B either ran on the same node or ran on different nodes

questions.explanation: Happens-before is an expression of causality. If A happened before B, B might have known about A, built on it, or depended on it. If neither happened before the other, they are concurrent: there is no causal link and neither knew about the other. Because concurrent operations exist, causality is a partial rather than a total order. Conflicts and node placement are separate questions.

questions.question: Snapshot isolation lets a transaction read from a 'consistent snapshot'. What does 'consistent' mean here?

options.text: Consistent with causality: if the snapshot contains an answer, it also contains the question being answered
All replicas hold byte-for-byte identical copies of the snapshot at the moment the transaction starts reading
The snapshot is linearizable, so it always includes the very latest writes committed anywhere in the database
The snapshot contains no writes at all from any transaction that ran concurrently with the reading transaction

questions.explanation: A consistent snapshot shows the database as of a single point in time, so it includes the effects of every operation that causally happened before that point and none that happened after. That makes it consistent with causality. Read skew (non-repeatable reads) means reading data in a state that violates causality. A snapshot is deliberately not linearizable, since it excludes newer writes.

questions.question: Two on-call doctors each check that the other is still on call, and then each goes off call in a separate transaction, leaving nobody on call (write skew). How can this anomaly be described in causal terms?

options.text: Each decision to go off call depended on observing who was on call, which the other transaction then invalidated
Both transactions wrote the same row, so it is really a lost update with no causal element involved in it at all
