Both transactions read from stale replicas of the shift table, so the anomaly is really just a case of read skew
Write skew has no causal interpretation, since the two transactions are independent and never see each other

questions.explanation: Each doctor's action (going off call) depended on what they had observed (that the other doctor was still on call). When the other transaction changes that premise, the action is based on outdated knowledge. Serializable snapshot isolation detects write skew by tracking exactly these causal dependencies between transactions. The doctors wrote different rows, so it is not a lost update.

questions.question: Alice sees a football result and exclaims it, and Bob, who heard her, then gets a stale result from the server. How is this linearizability violation described in causal terms?

options.text: Alice's exclamation causally depends on the score announcement, so after hearing it Bob should see the score
It is a pure concurrency anomaly with no causal element, since Alice and Bob reloaded at about the same time
It is a durability violation, because the database lost the final score after it had first been written
It is write skew between two readers of the same score, each of whom acted on an outdated premise

questions.explanation: The score announcement caused Alice's exclamation, which caused Bob's reload. Bob's query is therefore causally after the announcement, and a system that respects causality should show him the score. The causal link went through a channel the database could not see (Alice's voice), which is why linearizability, rather than ordinary database-internal causality tracking, is needed to guarantee the right answer.

questions.question: Which of the following are orderings that causality imposes on events?

options.text: Cause before effect, sending a message before receiving it, and a question before its answer
A lower physical timestamp before a higher one, whichever node's clock produced either timestamp
A write before every read that starts later in wall-clock time, even on unrelated keys
A leader's operations before any of its followers' operations, regardless of what they depend on

questions.explanation: Causality orders events by dependency: cause before effect, a message is sent before it is received, a question comes before its answer. Chains of causally dependent operations (one node reads data, writes something as a result, another node reads that and writes something else) define the causal order of the system, meaning what happened before what. Physical timestamps can contradict that order because of clock skew, a real-time ordering of unrelated operations is what linearizability adds rather than what causality requires, and a node's role as leader or follower says nothing about what an operation depended on.

questions.question: What is a system called that obeys the ordering imposed by causality, and which familiar mechanism provides it?

options.text: Causally consistent; snapshot isolation provides it
Linearizable; eventual consistency provides it
Eventually consistent; last-write-wins provides it
Serializable; read committed isolation provides it

questions.explanation: A system that obeys causal ordering is causally consistent. Snapshot isolation provides causal consistency: when you read from a snapshot and see some data, you can also see any data that causally precedes it (unless it has since been deleted). Eventual consistency and last-write-wins make no causal promise, and read committed does not provide serializability.

questions.question: What distinguishes a total order from a partial order?

options.text: In a total order every pair of elements is comparable; in a partial order some pairs are incomparable
In a partial order every pair of elements is comparable; in a total order some pairs are left incomparable
Both allow every pair to be compared, and they differ only in the direction in which comparisons run
A total order allows incomparable pairs, provided that the elements in each such pair are equal

questions.explanation: In a total order you can always say which of two elements is greater: natural numbers are totally ordered, so 13 is greater than 5. Sets ordered by inclusion are only partially ordered: one set is greater than another if it contains all of the other's elements, but {a, b} and {b, c} are incomparable because neither contains the other. Causality is a partial order for the same reason: concurrent events cannot be compared.

questions.question: Which consistency model imposes a total order on all operations, and which only a partial order?

options.text: Linearizability gives a total order of all operations; causality gives only a partial order
Causality orders all operations totally, whereas linearizability orders them only partially
Both of them impose a total order, in which every pair of operations can be compared
Both of them impose only a partial order, in which concurrent operations stay incomparable

questions.explanation: In a linearizable system all operations fall on one timeline: since there is effectively one copy and every operation is atomic, for any two operations one happened first, and there are no concurrent operations. Causality orders only operations that are causally related; concurrent operations are incomparable, so it defines a partial order.

questions.question: If you draw the history of a system on a timeline, what does concurrency look like?

options.text: The timeline branches and merges again, and operations on different branches are incomparable
A single straight line that simply has gaps between some of the operations along the way
A closed loop in which every operation precedes, and is preceded by, every other operation
A straight line on which concurrent operations are drawn at exactly the same point in time

questions.explanation: A linearizable history is one straight line. Concurrency means the timeline branches and later merges, and operations on different branches are concurrent, meaning incomparable. Version histories in Git look the same way: commits often follow one another in a straight line, but concurrent work creates branches, and merges combine them. That branching graph is the picture of a partial order of causal dependencies.

questions.question: What is the relationship between linearizability and causal consistency?

options.text: Linearizability implies causality: every linearizable system preserves causal order, but not vice versa
Causal consistency implies linearizability: every causally consistent system is linearizable, but not vice versa
Linearizability is strictly weaker than causality, since a linearizable history may still expose stale values
The two are exactly equivalent guarantees, described under different names in different research communities

questions.explanation: Any linearizable system preserves causality automatically, even across multiple communication channels, without passing timestamps between components. That is what makes linearizable systems simple to understand. The converse does not hold: a causally consistent system can avoid linearizability and its costs, since linearizability can harm performance and availability, especially with large network delays. Linearizability forbids stale reads, so it is the stronger guarantee.

questions.question: Why is causal consistency an attractive middle ground between linearizability and eventual consistency?

options.text: It preserves causality without linearizability's performance cost and stays available during network failures
Because it is weaker than eventual consistency, it is the cheapest model to implement on any replicated store
Because it must be implemented on top of linearizable storage, it inherits linearizability's guarantees
Because it is the strongest consistency model of all, it removes every anomaly that replication can cause

questions.explanation: Causal consistency is the strongest consistency model that does not slow down because of network delays and that remains available during network failures; CAP does not apply to it. Many systems that seem to need linearizability really only need causal consistency. At the time of writing, databases that preserve causality with near-eventual-consistency performance were an active but young research direction, with challenges remaining. It is stronger than eventual consistency but weaker than linearizability.

questions.question: In a causally consistent replicated system, what must a replica do before processing an operation?

options.text: Ensure that all causally preceding operations have already been processed, waiting if any are missing
Process all operations strictly in the order of the physical timestamps attached to them by their origin nodes
Process all operations strictly in the order in which they happen to arrive at the replica over the network
Process operations in any order it likes, since the causal order can always be restored afterward by sorting

questions.explanation: Causality is a partial order: concurrent operations may be processed in any order, but if one operation happened before another, every replica must process them in that order. So a replica must check that all operations the new one depends on have been applied; if a predecessor is missing, the later operation waits. Timestamp or arrival order can invert real dependencies.

questions.question: To determine causal dependencies between operations, what must the system be able to describe, and what analogy captures this?

options.text: The knowledge a node had when it issued a write, like asking whether a CEO knew about X when deciding Y
The wall-clock time at which each write was issued, like timing runners in a race precisely with a stopwatch
The network topology connecting the nodes, like following a road map to see which nodes can reach each other
The quorum membership in force at each write, like counting the votes cast for each candidate in an election

questions.explanation: Causality is about knowledge: if a node had already seen value X when it issued write Y, then X and Y may be causally related. The questions resemble a fraud investigation: did the CEO know about X at the time they made decision Y? Wall-clock times, topology, and quorum membership do not tell you what a node had seen.

questions.question: Detecting concurrent writes to a single key (for example with version vectors) is one form of causality tracking. What must causal consistency track beyond that?

options.text: Causal dependencies across the entire database, not just within one key
Only per-key dependencies, exactly as concurrent-write detection does
The physical clock reading of every node at the moment each write was issued
The order in which a single designated leader received every write in the cluster

questions.explanation: Concurrent-write detection in a leaderless datastore tracks causality for one key, to prevent lost updates. Causal consistency goes further: it must track dependencies across all keys in the database, because a write to one key may depend on a read of another. Version vectors can be generalized to do this. Physical clocks and a single leader are not what causal tracking relies on.

questions.question: In a causally consistent database, what must an application include when it writes a value that was derived from a prior read?

options.text: The version of the data that the application previously read
The current replication lag measured at the coordinator
The identity of the replica that served the earlier read
The transaction isolation level configured for the database

questions.explanation: To determine causal order, the database must know which version of the data the application read before writing. That is why a version number from a prior read is passed back to the database with the write. A similar idea appears in serializable snapshot isolation, where the database checks at commit whether the data a transaction read is still up to date. Replica identity, lag, and isolation level do not identify the causal predecessor.

questions.question: Why is explicitly tracking all causal dependencies often impractical?

options.text: Clients read lots of data before writing, and it is unclear which reads a write depends on, so tracking all is costly
It requires synchronized physical clocks on every node, which are not available in practice in most real datacenters
It requires all writes to pass through a single leader, which limits the write throughput the whole system can achieve
Dependencies can form cycles that no algorithm can resolve, so a consistent causal order often does not exist

questions.explanation: In many applications a client reads a lot of data before writing, and it is not clear whether the write depends on all or only some of those reads. Explicitly tracking everything that was read would mean large overhead. Causal dependencies never form cycles (a cause always precedes its effect), and no synchronized clocks or single leader are needed. Sequence numbers or timestamps offer a compact alternative: a few bytes per operation that provide a total order, which can be made consistent with causality.

questions.question: What is a logical clock?

options.text: An algorithm generating sequence numbers to identify operations, usually counters incremented per operation
A physical time-of-day clock that is synchronized with NTP so that its error stays within a known bound
A high-resolution hardware timer on each node that measures elapsed time precisely in nanoseconds
A clock that reads the current time from a GPS receiver, avoiding the drift of ordinary quartz oscillators

questions.explanation: A timestamp need not come from a time-of-day (physical) clock, which has many problems such as drift and skew. A logical clock is an algorithm that generates a sequence of numbers to identify operations, usually counters incremented for each operation. Its values are compact and can be compared to order operations, without claiming to measure real time.

questions.question: Sequence numbers can be generated in a total order that is consistent with causality. What does that mean?

options.text: If A causally happened before B, A gets the lower number; concurrent operations may be ordered arbitrarily
Concurrent operations are left unordered, so some pairs of their sequence numbers cannot be compared at all
The total order captures less information than the causal partial order, since it discards some dependencies
The total order imposes exactly the ordering that causality requires, and not a single comparison more than that

questions.explanation: Consistency with causality is a promise: whenever A causally precedes B, A has the lower sequence number. Concurrent operations still receive distinct comparable numbers, ordered arbitrarily. Such an order captures all the causal information but imposes more ordering than causality strictly requires. By contrast, a total order from random UUIDs is valid but useless, because it says nothing about which operation actually happened first.

questions.question: How does a database with single-leader replication obtain a total order of writes that is consistent with causality?

options.text: The leader increments a counter for each operation, so the replication log defines the order
Every node synchronizes its clock with NTP, and writes are then sorted by their wall-clock timestamps
A version vector is attached to every write, and replicas sort the writes by comparing those vectors
It cannot obtain one, because single-leader replication is not causally consistent even for followers

questions.explanation: The leader assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number to each operation in its replication log, so the log defines a total order of writes consistent with causality. A follower that applies writes in log order is always in a causally consistent state, even if it lags behind the leader. No clock synchronization is needed.

questions.question: Without a single leader (for example in a multi-leader, leaderless, or partitioned database), which methods are used in practice to generate unique, approximately increasing sequence numbers? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Give each node its own disjoint pattern of numbers, such as odd values on one node and even values on another
Attach a sufficiently high-resolution timestamp from each node's physical clock
Preallocate nonoverlapping blocks of sequence numbers to each node
Generate a random UUID for each operation and compare UUIDs lexicographically

questions.explanation: Three methods are common: per-node disjoint number spaces (for example reserving bits for a node ID), physical-clock timestamps, and preallocated blocks such as 1 to 1,000 for node A and 1,001 to 2,000 for node B. All perform better and scale better than routing every operation through a single leader's counter, and all produce unique, roughly increasing numbers. Random UUIDs are unique but not approximately increasing.

optionExplanations.a: Disjoint patterns such as odd and even numbers, or a node ID embedded in some bits, prevent two nodes from generating the same number without consulting a leader. They provide uniqueness but not a causal order.
optionExplanations.b: Each node can timestamp operations locally; with high enough resolution the timestamps may be enough to totally order operations, which is what last-write-wins relies on. Clock skew can still invert causal order.
optionExplanations.c: Allocating separate number blocks lets a node issue many identifiers independently until its block runs low, then claim a new one. Numeric order need not match the order of events.
optionExplanations.d: Random UUIDs are unique, but comparing them gives an arbitrary order unrelated to time, so they are not approximately increasing sequence numbers and say nothing about which operation happened first.

questions.question: Odd/even per-node counters, physical-clock timestamps, and preallocated blocks of sequence numbers can all generate unique numbers without a single leader. Which statements about their shortcomings are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: None of them is guaranteed to generate numbers consistent with causality across nodes
With odd/even counters one node's counter can lag the other's, so comparing an odd and an even number does not reveal which happened first
With physical timestamps, clock skew can give a causally later operation a lower timestamp
With block allocation, a causally later operation always receives the higher number

questions.explanation: All three generators give unique, approximately increasing numbers, but none correctly captures the order of operations across different nodes. Counters on different nodes advance at different rates; physical clocks are skewed; and a node using a low block may issue a smaller number after another node issued a larger one. So a causally later operation can receive a lower number in every scheme.

optionExplanations.a: Each scheme generates numbers independently per node, so none can see causal dependencies between nodes. A dependent later operation may get a numerically smaller identifier.
optionExplanations.b: If one node processes more operations per second, its counter runs ahead of the other's. An odd and an even number then cannot tell you which operation causally happened first.
optionExplanations.c: Physical timestamps inherit clock skew, so an event on a node with a slow clock can sort before an event it depends on. Higher precision does not fix a clock that is offset.
optionExplanations.d: Blocks guarantee only that numbers do not collide. One operation may get a number from 1,001 to 2,000 and a causally later operation a number from 1 to 1,000, so the later one can be lower.

questions.question: Who proposed Lamport timestamps, when, and what does a Lamport timestamp consist of?

options.text: Leslie Lamport, in 1978; a pair of (counter, node ID)
Leslie Lamport, in 1998; a single global counter shared by the whole system
Leslie Lamport, in 1978; a vector containing one counter per node
Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson, in 1985; a wall-clock time plus a node ID

questions.explanation: Leslie Lamport proposed them in 1978, in one of the most-cited papers in distributed systems. Each node has a unique ID and a counter of operations processed, and a timestamp is the pair (counter, node ID). Timestamps compare by counter first, then by node ID, so they are unique and totally ordered. A vector of counters is a version vector, and no physical clock is involved.

questions.question: What is the key idea that makes Lamport timestamps consistent with causality?

options.text: Every node and client tracks the maximum counter it has seen and sends it on each request; a node receiving a larger value jumps its counter to it
Each node increments its counter only for its own local operations, deliberately ignoring the counter values used by any other node in the system
Each node periodically synchronizes its counter with a central NTP server, so that all of the counters stay within a known bound of each other
Each node resets its counter to zero at the start of every request it handles, so that counters from different requests never interfere with one another

questions.explanation: Without this rule, Lamport timestamps would be no better than independent per-node counters. Every node and client remembers the largest counter value it has seen and includes it on every request. When a node receives a request or response carrying a larger maximum than its own counter, it immediately advances its counter to that maximum. For instance, if a client received counter 5 from node 2 and then contacts node 1, whose counter is 1, node 1 jumps to 5 and gives its next operation 6. Every causal dependency thus produces a larger timestamp.

questions.question: How do Lamport timestamps differ from version vectors?

options.text: Version vectors can tell whether two operations are concurrent; Lamport timestamps always impose a total order but are more compact
They are the same mechanism described under two different names, one used in databases and the other in distributed-systems theory
Lamport timestamps can detect whether two operations are concurrent, while version vectors always impose a single total order on them
Version vectors are the more compact of the two, while Lamport timestamps carry more information about causal relationships between nodes

questions.explanation: Version vectors can distinguish whether two operations are concurrent or one causally depends on the other. Lamport timestamps always enforce a total order, so from two Lamport timestamps alone you cannot tell whether the operations were concurrent or causally related. Their advantage is compactness: one counter and a node ID instead of one counter per node.

questions.question: Two users concurrently try to register the same username, and every operation carries a Lamport timestamp. Once all the creation operations have been collected, what rule would pick the winner?

options.text: The claim with the lower Lamport timestamp wins, and the other fails
The claim with the higher Lamport timestamp wins, since it is more recent
Both claims succeed, and the two accounts are merged afterward
The node with the lower ID always wins, regardless of the timestamps

questions.explanation: Because Lamport timestamps are totally ordered, after collecting all username-creation operations you can always compare them: the one with the lower timestamp grabbed the name first and wins, and the other fails. The comparison is always valid. The catch is that this works only after the fact; a node deciding at the moment a request arrives cannot yet know about every competing claim.

questions.question: Lamport timestamps can pick a winner among concurrent username claims once all claims are collected. Why is this insufficient when a node must answer a registration request immediately?

options.text: It cannot know if another node is concurrently claiming the name with a lower timestamp; asking every node stalls if one is down
Lamport timestamps issued by different nodes are not comparable with each other, so no winner can ever be chosen among the claims
Physical clocks would be needed instead of Lamport timestamps to order the claims, and physical clocks drift too much to be useful
Lamport counters overflow quickly under high write rates, so the timestamps of concurrent claims often collide

questions.explanation: At the moment a request arrives, the node does not know whether another node is concurrently creating an account with the same name, or what timestamp that other operation will carry. To be sure, it would have to ask every other node; if any node has failed or is unreachable, the system grinds to a halt, which is not fault-tolerant. The total order only emerges after all operations are collected, so unseen operations may still need to be inserted earlier in it. Lamport timestamps from different nodes are always comparable, and including the node ID makes every timestamp unique, so neither comparability nor collisions are the problem.

questions.question: To implement a uniqueness constraint such as unique usernames, what do you need in addition to a total ordering of operations?

options.text: Knowing when the order is final, so no node can insert an earlier conflicting claim
Physical clocks synchronized across all the nodes to within a bounded, known error
Version vectors attached to every operation in addition to the Lamport timestamps
A random tie-breaker, so that equal Lamport counters on two nodes never collide

questions.explanation: A total order is not enough by itself: you also need to know when it is finalized. If you are sure that no other node can insert a claim for the same username ahead of yours in the total order, you can safely declare your operation successful. Ties between equal Lamport counters are already broken by the node ID, and neither synchronized clocks nor version vectors tell you when the order is final. This idea of knowing when the total order is final is captured by total order broadcast.

questions.question: How does single-leader replication determine a total order of operations, and what challenges does that approach face?

options.text: One leader sequences all operations on a single CPU core; the challenges are scaling beyond one leader and failing over
It synchronizes all the nodes' physical clocks; the challenges are clock drift and the skew between different nodes
It holds a quorum vote on every single operation; the challenges are the added latency and reduced availability
It attaches version vectors to every write; the challenges are the size of the vectors and the cost of comparing them

questions.explanation: Single-leader replication chooses one node as leader and sequences all operations on a single CPU core on that leader, which trivially gives a total order. The challenges are how to scale when throughput exceeds what one leader can handle, and how to fail over if the leader fails without creating competing orders. In the distributed systems literature this problem is known as total order broadcast, or atomic broadcast.

questions.question: Total order broadcast (also called atomic broadcast) is a protocol for exchanging messages between nodes. Which two safety properties must it always satisfy?

options.text: Reliable delivery to all nodes, and delivery in the same order on every node
Delivery within a fixed time bound, and acknowledgments in send order
At-most-once delivery to each node, and ordering of causally related messages only
Exactly-once delivery, and ordering by each sender's physical clock

questions.explanation: Reliable delivery means no messages are lost: if a message is delivered to one node, it is delivered to all nodes. Totally ordered delivery means messages are delivered to every node in the same order. A correct algorithm must preserve both even when nodes or the network are faulty. Messages cannot be delivered while the network is interrupted, but the algorithm keeps retrying and, once the network is repaired, still delivers them in the correct order. There is no time bound.

questions.question: Which coordination services implement total order broadcast internally, hinting at a strong connection between total order broadcast and consensus?

options.text: ZooKeeper and etcd
Cassandra and Riak
Memcached and Redis
DNS servers with multiple layers of caching

questions.explanation: Consensus services such as ZooKeeper and etcd actually implement total order broadcast. That is a hint that the two problems are closely connected, and in fact total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus. Leaderless stores, caches, and DNS do not provide fault-tolerant total order broadcast.

questions.question: Why is total order broadcast exactly what you need for database replication?

options.text: If every message is a write and every replica applies the same writes in the same order, the replicas stay consistent
Because it guarantees that replication lag between any two nodes stays within a bounded, configurable number of seconds
Because it removes the need for any kind of leader or sequencer, letting every node accept writes completely independently
Because it makes every write naturally idempotent when it is replayed, so duplicates never affect the state of a replica

questions.explanation: If each message represents a write to the database and every replica applies the same writes in the same order, the replicas remain consistent with each other, apart from temporary replication lag. This principle is called state machine replication. Similarly, if each message is a deterministic transaction run as a stored procedure, processing them in the same order on every node gives serializable transactions. Total order broadcast is asynchronous, so it does not bound lag.

questions.question: What property about when the order is fixed makes total order broadcast stronger than ordering by timestamps?

options.text: The order is fixed at delivery: no message may be inserted at an earlier position once later ones are delivered
The order is fixed earlier, when each sender attaches a timestamp to its message before any delivery happens at all
The order is never fixed, so nodes remain free to re-sort the messages they have already delivered whenever needed
The order is fixed by physical timestamps from each sender, which makes the two approaches exactly equivalent overall

questions.explanation: With total order broadcast, the order is fixed at the time messages are delivered: no node may retroactively insert a message into an earlier position after subsequent messages have been delivered. With timestamp ordering, a message with a lower timestamp from another node might still turn up, so you never know when the order is final. Another way to see total order broadcast is as an append-only log that every node reads in the same sequence.

questions.question: How can total order broadcast be used to implement a lock service that issues fencing tokens?

options.text: Append each lock request to the log; requests are numbered in log order, and that increasing number is the token
Grant each lock by comparing physical timestamps across nodes, and use the winning timestamp as the fencing token
Run a separate two-phase commit for each acquisition, and use that transaction's global ID as the fencing token
Grant each lock by majority vote among the clients, and use the number of votes received as the fencing token

questions.explanation: Every request to acquire the lock is appended to the log as a message, and messages are sequentially numbered in log order. Because that number increases monotonically, it can serve as a fencing token: a storage service can reject requests carrying an older token than one it has already seen. In ZooKeeper this sequence number is called the zxid. Physical timestamps are not monotonic across nodes, so they cannot replace it.

questions.question: Is linearizability the same as total order broadcast?

options.text: Not quite: broadcast fixes the delivery order but is asynchronous, while linearizability is a recency guarantee
Yes: the two provide exactly the same guarantees, and the different names come from different research traditions
No: broadcast is the recency guarantee, while linearizability is the asynchronous one with no timing promise
No: linearizability orders only the concurrent writes, while total order broadcast orders only the reads

questions.explanation: Both involve a total order, but total order broadcast promises only that messages are delivered reliably and in the same order; it says nothing about when, so one node may lag behind others. Linearizability is a recency guarantee: a read sees the latest value written. They are closely linked: linearizable storage can be built on total order broadcast and vice versa. Formally, a plain read-write register is easier, while a register with compare-and-set or increment-and-get is equivalent to consensus, as is total order broadcast.

questions.question: A linearizable compare-and-set for claiming usernames can be built on total order broadcast used as an append-only log. Which steps belong to that procedure? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Append a message to the log tentatively claiming the username
Wait until the appended message is delivered back to you
Succeed only if the first message in the log claiming that username is your own; otherwise abort
Before appending, query every other node to check for concurrent claims

questions.explanation: The log gives every node the same order of claims. A client appends a tentative claim, reads the log until its own message comes back, and then checks: if the first claim for that username is its own, the claim succeeds (perhaps recorded with another log message) and is acknowledged; otherwise it aborts. Because all nodes see the same order, they all agree on the winner. Acknowledging before the message comes back would lose linearizability.

optionExplanations.a: Appending the claim places it into the single order observed by every node. It is only tentative because an earlier claim for the same username may already be in the log.
optionExplanations.b: Waiting for your own entry to be delivered ensures you have seen every claim ordered before it. Acknowledging earlier would let an earlier competing claim, not yet seen, win after you had already reported success.
optionExplanations.c: First claim in the shared log wins, so every node picks the same owner. A follow-up log entry may record the commit, while later claims abort deterministically.
optionExplanations.d: Querying every node before appending is unnecessary and racy: another claim may appear after the check but before the append, and the check stalls if a node is unreachable. The log order itself decides.

questions.question: When a username claim is decided by appending it to a totally ordered log and checking whether it is the first claim for that name, why do all nodes agree on the outcome?

options.text: Log entries are delivered to all nodes in the same order, so all agree which conflicting claim came first
The log order is established by synchronized physical clocks on every node, so all nodes sort claims the same way
Each node individually confirms the outcome of every claim with every other node before it accepts the result
The log is stored on a single designated node, and all the other nodes simply defer to whatever that node says

questions.explanation: Because every node sees the log entries in the same order, all nodes agree on which of several concurrent writes came first; choosing the first as the winner and aborting the rest means every node agrees on whether each write committed. This makes writes linearizable. Reads from a store that is updated asynchronously from the log may still be stale, which gives sequential consistency (timeline consistency), slightly weaker than linearizability.

questions.question: Writes built on a totally ordered log can be linearizable, while reads from a store that is updated asynchronously from the log may be stale. Which techniques make reads linearizable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Append a message for the read to the log, and perform the read when that message is delivered back
Fetch the latest log position in a linearizable way, wait until entries up to it are delivered, then read
Read from a replica that is updated synchronously on every write
Read from any replica, because log order alone guarantees the replica is current

questions.explanation: There are three options. Sequencing the read through the log fixes the point in time at which it happens (etcd's quorum reads work somewhat like this). Querying the latest log position linearizably and waiting until it has been applied is the idea behind ZooKeeper's sync(). Reading from a synchronously updated replica works because it is guaranteed up to date (as in chain replication). An arbitrary replica may lag, because delivery is asynchronous.

optionExplanations.a: Putting the read itself into the ordered log places it after every write delivered before it. When the read's message comes back, local state reflects exactly that prefix.
optionExplanations.b: A linearizable read of the current end of the log acts as a recency barrier. Waiting until that position has been applied ensures the local replica has caught up before it serves data.
optionExplanations.c: A replica that is updated synchronously with every write cannot miss a completed write, so it can serve current reads without extra coordination.
optionExplanations.d: Total order broadcast is asynchronous, so a replica may be behind the end of the agreed log. Same order does not mean up to date, so reading any replica can return stale data.

questions.question: To build total order broadcast from linearizable storage, what do you need?

options.text: A linearizable integer register with an atomic increment-and-get (or compare-and-set) operation
A synchronized physical clock on each node that attaches a precise timestamp to every message
A version vector maintained separately by each node and attached to every message it sends
A Lamport clock on each node, with recipients delivering messages as soon as they arrive

questions.explanation: For every message, increment-and-get the linearizable integer and attach the returned value as the message's sequence number. Then send the message to all nodes, resending lost messages, and have recipients deliver messages consecutively by sequence number. Because the register hands out numbers with no gaps, every node delivers the same sequence. Physical clocks, version vectors, and Lamport clocks do not provide gap-free numbering.

questions.question: Total order broadcast is built by tagging each message with a number from a linearizable increment-and-get register. A node has delivered message 4 and then receives message 6. What must it do, and why?

options.text: Wait for message 5 before delivering 6, because the register's numbers have no gaps
Deliver message 6 immediately, since the order only has to be respected per sender
Discard message 6, since any message that arrives out of order is treated as invalid
Deliver message 6 at once, and then deliver message 5 later if it ever does arrive

questions.explanation: Numbers from a linearizable increment-and-get register form a sequence with no gaps, so seeing 6 after 4 proves that message 5 exists and has not yet arrived; the node must wait for it. With Lamport timestamps this inference is impossible, because their values can have gaps: you cannot tell whether a missing number corresponds to a real message. This is the key difference between total order broadcast and timestamp ordering.

questions.question: Why is it hard to build a linearizable integer register with an atomic increment-and-get operation?

options.text: Keeping it on one node is easy; surviving that node's failure or disconnection requires consensus
Atomic increments on one node contend for a lock, so throughput collapses when many clients use it
It cannot be done at all unless the network is fully synchronous, with a known bound on every message delay
It only needs a synchronized physical clock on every node, which replaces the counter with a timestamp

questions.explanation: If nothing ever failed, you could keep the integer in a variable on one node. The difficulty is handling network interruptions to that node and restoring the value when the node fails. Thinking hard about fault-tolerant linearizable sequence-number generators inevitably leads to a consensus algorithm. That is no coincidence: a linearizable compare-and-set or increment-and-get register and total order broadcast are both provably equivalent to consensus. Lock contention on a single node is a throughput concern, not the fundamental difficulty, and neither fully synchronous networks nor physical clocks are required.

questions.question: Why have many broken distributed systems been built around consensus?

options.text: It looks simple, getting several nodes to agree, but it is subtle in the presence of faults
Consensus is needed only for ordering, and ordering is easy with high-resolution physical timestamps
Consensus needs perfectly synchronized clocks, which few datacenters can provide
Consensus is impossible in practice, so every implementation is necessarily broken

questions.explanation: Informally, the goal of consensus is just to get several nodes to agree on something, which seems easy. Many broken systems have been built in the mistaken belief that it is. Even researchers took decades to understand the subtleties, with many misunderstandings along the way. Consensus is achievable in practice (FLP impossibility applies only to a very restrictive model), it does not depend on synchronized clocks, and physical timestamps cannot order events reliably because of clock skew.

questions.question: Why is consensus best studied after replication, transactions, system models, linearizability, and total order broadcast?

options.text: Because appreciating its subtleties requires that prerequisite knowledge
Because it matters less in practice than those other topics do
Because consensus algorithms were invented only very recently
Because consensus matters only for systems with hundreds of nodes or more

questions.explanation: Consensus is one of the most important and fundamental problems in distributed computing, but it is subtle. Understanding why it is hard, and why solutions look the way they do, relies on concepts such as replication, transactions, failure models, linearizability, and total order broadcast. The algorithms are decades old (Paxos and Viewstamped Replication date from the 1980s and 1990s), and consensus matters even for three-node clusters.

questions.question: In a database with single-leader replication, why is consensus needed?

options.text: Because all nodes must agree on which node is the leader, especially during failover
Because followers must vote on the order of every write the leader sends
Because clients must agree on which replica each of them reads from
Because every read must be confirmed by a majority of followers before the leader returns it

questions.explanation: All nodes must agree on who the leader is. The leadership may be contested if some nodes cannot communicate with others because of a network fault, and a bad failover can result in split brain, where two nodes both believe themselves to be leader. Both then accept writes, data diverges, and data is lost. Consensus prevents this. Once leadership is settled, the leader alone decides the order of writes, reads from the leader need no follower vote, and clients do not need to agree on replicas.

questions.question: What is the atomic commit problem?

options.text: Getting all nodes in a transaction to agree on one outcome: either all commit or all abort
Getting all nodes to agree on which isolation level each distributed transaction should use
Getting all nodes to agree on the order of the individual writes within one transaction
Getting all nodes to agree on which partition holds each row that a transaction touches

questions.explanation: In a database where transactions span several nodes or partitions, a transaction may fail on some nodes and succeed on others. To keep transaction atomicity, all nodes must agree on the outcome: all abort if anything goes wrong, or all commit if nothing does. This is an instance of consensus. It is formalized slightly differently (commit is allowed only if every participant votes yes), but atomic commit and consensus are reducible to each other.

questions.question: Which result proves that no deterministic algorithm can always reach consensus in a fully asynchronous system where a node may crash?

options.text: The FLP result of Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson
The CAP theorem as formalized by Gilbert and Lynch
The Attiya and Welch bound on linearizable latency
Lamport's happens-before relation for distributed events

questions.explanation: The FLP result proves that there is no algorithm that is always able to reach consensus if there is a risk that a node may crash. It holds in the asynchronous system model, which assumes a deterministic algorithm that cannot use clocks or timeouts. If the algorithm may use timeouts or some other way of suspecting crashed nodes (even if the suspicion is sometimes wrong), or even random numbers, consensus becomes solvable. So distributed systems can usually achieve consensus in practice. CAP and the Attiya-Welch bound concern linearizability, not consensus.

questions.question: What is two-phase commit's relationship to consensus?

options.text: 2PC is the most common way of solving atomic commit, and is a kind of consensus algorithm, but not a good one
2PC is a strong fault-tolerant consensus algorithm, which is why ZooKeeper and etcd build on it
2PC has nothing to do with consensus, since it only ever decides between committing and aborting a transaction
2PC has largely been replaced by consensus algorithms in databases and application servers

questions.explanation: Two-phase commit is the most common way to solve atomic commit and is implemented in many databases, messaging systems, and application servers. It is a kind of consensus algorithm, but a poor one: it does not satisfy termination, because participants may block forever if the coordinator fails. ZooKeeper and etcd use better algorithms (Zab and Raft), and 2PC is still widely used.

questions.question: How is atomic commit implemented for a transaction that executes on a single database node?

options.text: The storage engine durably writes the data, then appends a commit record; once that record is on disk, it is committed
The storage engine takes a lock on every row the transaction touches, and releasing those locks is what commits it
The storage engine writes the commit record to disk first, and only after that writes the transaction's actual data
The storage engine's worker threads each vote on the transaction, and it commits if a majority of them approve it

questions.explanation: On a single node the storage engine makes the transaction's writes durable (typically in a write-ahead log), then appends a commit record. If the database crashes, recovery checks the log: with a commit record on disk the transaction is committed, without one its writes are rolled back. The deciding moment is when the disk finishes writing the commit record, so a single device makes the commit atomic. Writing the commit record before the data would allow a committed transaction with missing data.

questions.question: Which is an example of a transaction that requires atomic commit across multiple nodes?

options.text: A multi-object transaction in a partitioned database, or a write whose secondary index entry lives on another node
A single-row update on a database that runs entirely on one node, with its write-ahead log on the local disk
A read-only query against a single replica of a database, returning rows that were committed some time earlier
A batch job that writes all of its output to a single local file and replaces the previous file when it finishes

questions.explanation: Atomic commit across nodes is needed whenever one transaction's writes land on several nodes: a multi-object transaction in a partitioned database, or a write whose term-partitioned secondary index entry lives on a different node from the primary data. Most NoSQL distributed datastores do not support such distributed transactions, but various clustered relational systems do. Single-node writes and read-only queries need no cross-node commit protocol.

questions.question: Why is it not sufficient to send a commit request to all nodes in a distributed transaction and have each commit independently? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some nodes may detect a constraint violation or conflict, making an abort necessary, while other nodes are successfully able to commit
Some of the commit requests might be lost in the network, eventually aborting due to a timeout, while other commit requests get through
Some nodes may crash before the commit record is fully written and roll back on recovery, while others successfully commit
The participants would deadlock, each waiting for another to commit first, so no node could ever finish its commit

questions.explanation: Independent commit requests can be lost, rejected by a constraint check, or interrupted by a crash. Without a prepare-and-decide protocol, some participants may commit while others abort, permanently splitting the transaction.

optionExplanations.a: A participant may reject because of a local constraint or concurrency conflict while another commits successfully. Independent decisions would then violate all-or-nothing atomicity.
optionExplanations.b: Message loss can make one participant time out and abort even though another receives the same commit request and commits. Retrying cannot safely infer the missing global decision.
optionExplanations.c: A crash before a durable commit record may roll one participant back on recovery while another has committed. Prepare records and one coordinator decision prevent this split outcome.
optionExplanations.d: Deadlock is possible in transactions but is not the fundamental reason independent commit messages fail. The essential problem is inconsistent outcomes under rejection, loss, or crash.

questions.question: In a distributed transaction, when may a node commit, and why must commits be irrevocable?

options.text: Only once sure all other nodes will commit, because committed data becomes visible and others may rely on it
Independently, aborting again later if another node fails, because aborts are cheap and easy to propagate
At any time it likes, because commits can still be revoked within a short, bounded window after they happen
Once a majority of nodes confirm, because the abort of a minority of participants can safely be ignored

questions.explanation: Once a transaction commits on one node it cannot be retracted if it turns out to have aborted elsewhere, so a node may commit only when it is sure every other participant will commit too. Commits must be irrevocable because committed data becomes visible to other transactions, which may build on it; retroactively aborting would invalidate them as well. (A separate compensating transaction can undo effects later, but that is the application's concern.) Majority rule would break all-or-nothing atomicity.

questions.question: What is two-phase commit (2PC)?

options.text: An algorithm for atomic transaction commit across multiple nodes, so that all commit or all abort
A transaction isolation level that provides serializability by running transactions in a fixed order
A replication protocol that ships the leader's log to followers in two phases, first data then commits
A locking protocol that acquires all locks in one phase and releases them all in a second phase

questions.explanation: Two-phase commit ensures that either all nodes in a distributed transaction commit or all abort. It is used internally by some databases and exposed to applications as XA transactions (supported, for example, by the Java Transaction API) or WS-AtomicTransaction for SOAP web services. Do not confuse it with two-phase locking (2PL), which acquires and releases locks to provide serializable isolation; the two are entirely separate concepts.

questions.question: What component does two-phase commit introduce that does not normally appear in single-node transactions?

options.text: A coordinator, also called a transaction manager
A quorum of voters, always deployed as a separate cluster
A leader elected among the participants by majority vote
A message broker that relays writes between participants

questions.explanation: 2PC introduces a coordinator (transaction manager) that drives the prepare and commit phases. It is often implemented as a library inside the same application process that requests the transaction (for example embedded in a Java EE container), but it can also be a separate process or service; examples include Narayana, JOTM, BTM, and MSDTC. The coordinator is not elected and uses no quorum, which is part of why 2PC is not fault-tolerant.

questions.question: In a two-phase commit transaction, which nodes are the participants?

options.text: The database nodes on which the transaction reads and writes data
Only the coordinator and one designated primary database node
Every node in the cluster, whether or not it holds the transaction's data
Only the nodes that hold replicas of the coordinator's log

questions.explanation: A 2PC transaction begins with the application reading and writing data on multiple database nodes, as normal; these nodes are the participants. When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator sends each participant a prepare request asking whether it can commit. If all reply yes, the coordinator sends commit in phase 2; if any replies no, it sends abort to all.

questions.question: Two-phase commit is often compared to a traditional wedding ceremony. Which part of the ceremony corresponds to the prepare phase?

options.text: The minister asking the bride and groom individually whether they want to marry, and each answering 'I do'
The minister pronouncing the couple married in front of all the guests once both vows have been spoken aloud
The guests voting on whether the marriage should go ahead, with the ceremony continuing if most of them agree
The couple signing the marriage register after the ceremony, which is what makes the marriage legally binding

questions.explanation: The minister asks each partner individually (prepare) and receives 'I do' from both (yes votes). Having said 'I do', a partner cannot retract it, just as a participant that voted yes has given up the right to abort. The minister then pronounces them married (the commit decision), and the happy fact is broadcast to attendees. If either says no, the ceremony is aborted. Guests do not vote, so there is no quorum.

questions.question: Which of the following happen in two-phase commit before the coordinator makes its commit-or-abort decision? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The application obtains a globally unique transaction ID from the coordinator
The application opens single-node transactions on each participant, tagged with that ID
The coordinator asks every participant to prepare, aborting everywhere if any request fails or times out
The participants elect a leader among themselves before the prepare phase begins

questions.explanation: The application first gets a globally unique transaction ID, then does its reads and writes in single-node transactions on each participant, all tagged with that ID; anything going wrong at this stage lets the coordinator or any participant abort. When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator sends prepare requests tagged with the ID, and if any fails or times out, it sends abort to all participants. No election takes place.

optionExplanations.a: A globally unique transaction ID lets the coordinator and every participant associate retries, prepare records, and the final decision with one distributed transaction.
optionExplanations.b: Each participant performs its local reads and writes inside a transaction linked to the global ID. Until commit, this work is provisional and can still be aborted.
optionExplanations.c: The prepare request asks each participant whether it can promise to commit. Any failure, timeout, or no vote at this stage still allows a clean global abort.
optionExplanations.d: Two-phase commit uses a designated coordinator; participants do not elect a leader. Lack of an elected, fault-tolerant coordinator is precisely one of its weaknesses.

questions.question: In two-phase commit, which statements about the prepare votes, the commit point, and what follows are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each participant durably prepares, checks constraints, and votes yes or no
The coordinator records commit only if every participant votes yes
The coordinator retries its recorded decision until every participant applies it
If a prepared participant crashes, abort only the surviving participants

questions.explanation: The protocol has two crucial points of no return: when a participant votes 'yes' it promises that it will definitely be able to commit later, even though the coordinator may still choose to abort; and once the coordinator decides, that decision is irrevocable. Those promises ensure the atomicity of 2PC — single-node atomic commit lumps these two events into one, writing the commit record to the transaction log.

optionExplanations.a: A yes vote means the participant has durably recorded everything needed to commit later and has checked local constraints. It may no longer abort unilaterally after making that promise.
optionExplanations.b: Only unanimous yes votes permit the coordinator to durably record commit; any no vote leads to abort. Recording the decision is the coordinator's point of no return.
optionExplanations.c: After recording the decision, the coordinator can resend it until recovered participants acknowledge it. Retries are safe because every participant must apply the same irrevocable outcome.
optionExplanations.d: A prepared participant cannot be selectively abandoned or told to abort after global commit. Doing so only to survivors could make their result disagree with a recovering participant.

questions.question: In two-phase commit, a participant has received a prepare request and voted yes, and then the coordinator crashes. Why can the participant become stuck?

options.text: Having voted yes, it can no longer abort on its own and must wait for the coordinator's decision; it is in doubt
It can safely abort after a timeout, because the coordinator records an abort whenever it crashes mid-protocol
It can safely commit after a timeout, because it has already voted yes and every other participant must agree
It must ask a majority of the other participants to decide the outcome for it, as defined by the 2PC protocol

questions.explanation: If the coordinator fails before sending prepare requests, a participant can safely abort. But once it has voted yes, it has promised to commit if told to and can no longer abort on its own; it must hear from the coordinator whether the transaction committed or aborted. Until then the transaction is in doubt (uncertain). The coordinator may already have decided and recorded commit before crashing, so aborting alone is unsafe; committing alone is unsafe because another participant may have voted no; and asking other participants is not part of the 2PC protocol.

questions.question: In two-phase commit, databases 1 and 2 both vote yes. The coordinator decides to commit, sends the commit request to database 2, and crashes before sending it to database 1. Why can't database 1 safely decide on its own after a timeout?

options.text: Aborting would contradict database 2, which committed; committing alone is unsafe when another participant may have aborted
Database 1 has not yet durably written its prepared data, so it has nothing on disk to commit from
2PC forbids participants from using timeouts, so database 1 cannot even detect the coordinator's crash
It can ask database 2 for the outcome directly, which the 2PC protocol defines as the standard recovery path after a crash

questions.explanation: Database 1 cannot tell whether the coordinator decided to commit or abort. If it aborts after a timeout, it ends up inconsistent with database 2, which committed; in general, committing is also unsafe because another participant might have aborted. Having voted yes, database 1 has already written its transaction data durably, and timeouts are used in 2PC (for example to abort when a prepare request fails), so neither is the obstacle. Participants could in principle compare notes, but that is not part of 2PC. The only way 2PC can complete is to wait for the coordinator to recover and read its decision from its log, which is why the coordinator writes its decision to disk before sending it.

questions.question: Why is two-phase commit called a blocking atomic commit protocol, and why are nonblocking alternatives rarely used?

options.text: It can stall waiting for the coordinator to recover; nonblocking commit needs bounded delay or a perfect failure detector
It holds locks during the commit; three-phase commit avoids holding them and has become the usual replacement
It requires a unanimous yes vote; three-phase commit requires only a majority, which lets it proceed despite failures
It has two phases; adding a third phase removes the blocking in practice, so 3PC is widely deployed

questions.explanation: 2PC can get stuck waiting for a crashed coordinator. Three-phase commit has been proposed as a nonblocking alternative, but it assumes bounded network delay and bounded response times; with real unbounded delays and process pauses it cannot guarantee atomicity. In general, nonblocking atomic commit requires a perfect failure detector, and a timeout is not one, since a request can time out because of a network problem when no node has crashed. So 2PC continues to be used despite its coordinator problem.

questions.question: How large can the performance penalty of distributed transactions be, and where does much of it come from?

options.text: In MySQL, reportedly over 10 times slower than single-node ones, largely due to extra fsyncs and round-trips
They are typically only about 10% slower than single-node transactions, with the cost coming mainly from added network latency
They are usually about twice as slow as single-node transactions, with the cost coming mainly from lock contention on hot rows
About 50% slower, with almost all of the cost in the coordinator CPU work

questions.explanation: Some implementations carry a heavy penalty: distributed transactions in MySQL were reported to be over 10 times slower than single-node transactions. Much of the cost inherent in 2PC comes from the additional disk forcing (fsync) needed for crash recovery and from the additional network round-trips. Partly for these reasons, and for their operational problems, many cloud services choose not to implement distributed transactions.

questions.question: Distributed transactions are often lumped into one category. Which distinction between them actually matters?

options.text: Database-internal transactions versus heterogeneous transactions that span different technologies
Local transactions versus remote ones, distinguished by how many network hops each request crosses
Read-only transactions versus read-write transactions, distinguished by whether any data is modified
Short transactions versus long-running ones, distinguished by how many seconds each one stays open

questions.explanation: Database-internal distributed transactions run among nodes of the same distributed database (for example VoltDB or MySQL Cluster's NDB storage engine). Because they need not interoperate with anything else, they can use any protocol and technology-specific optimizations, and often work quite well. Heterogeneous transactions span different technologies, such as databases from different vendors or a database and a message broker, and are much more challenging.

questions.question: How can a heterogeneous distributed transaction achieve exactly-once message processing, and what limits it?

options.text: Commit the message acknowledgment and the database writes atomically; it works only if all affected systems support the same commit protocol
Deduplicate the messages in application code; this works only if every write the processing performs is idempotent and has no other side effects
Make the message broker retry delivery forever; this works only on a perfectly reliable network where retried messages are never duplicated
Process each message twice and compare the two results; this works only if the processing code is deterministic and has no external effects

questions.explanation: If the message acknowledgment and the database writes commit atomically in one distributed transaction, then either both happen or both are aborted, and the broker can safely redeliver an aborted message. The message is thus effectively processed exactly once, even if it took a few retries. This works only if every system affected by processing supports the same atomic commit protocol: if a side effect is sending an email via a server without 2PC support, the email might be sent several times.

questions.question: What is X/Open XA?

options.text: A standard, introduced in 1991, for implementing two-phase commit across heterogeneous technologies
A consensus protocol, introduced in 2001, that is used only inside Java EE application containers
A network wire protocol, introduced in 1981, for replicating data between mainframe databases
A message-broker standard, introduced in 1999, that guarantees exactly-once delivery of messages

questions.explanation: XA (eXtended Architecture) is a standard for two-phase commit across heterogeneous technologies, introduced in 1991 and widely implemented by relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, DB2, SQL Server, Oracle) and message brokers (ActiveMQ, HornetQ, MSMQ, IBM MQ). It is not a network protocol but a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator; in Java EE it is exposed through the Java Transaction API (JTA), supported by JDBC and JMS drivers.

questions.question: Where does an XA transaction coordinator typically run, and what happens if it crashes?

options.text: Often as a library in the application; if it dies, prepared participants stay in doubt until it restarts and reads its log
As a separate service replicated across several machines, so an application crash never affects any in-flight transaction
Inside each participant database server, so the coordinator survives application crashes and resolves transactions itself
As a stateless component that keeps no log at all, so no recovery is ever needed after the coordinator crashes

questions.explanation: The XA standard does not specify how the coordinator is implemented, but in practice it is often a library loaded into the application process, keeping its commit/abort decisions in a log on the local disk. If the application process or its machine dies, the coordinator goes with it, and participants with prepared transactions are stuck in doubt. The server must be restarted and the library must read its log before it can tell participants to commit or abort. The database cannot contact the coordinator directly, since all communication goes through its client library.

questions.question: In two-phase commit, why can't the rest of the system simply ignore a transaction that is stuck in doubt?

options.text: It keeps holding row locks until its outcome is known, blocking other transactions on those rows
It consumes memory on each participant until the database servers crash
It blocks the replication stream from the leader to all of its followers until the outcome is known
It forces every new transaction to wait until it resolves, even transactions that touch unrelated rows

questions.explanation: Transactions usually take row-level exclusive locks on rows they modify (and, under two-phase locking, shared locks on rows they read), and cannot release them until they commit or abort. An in-doubt transaction therefore holds its locks for as long as it is in doubt: 20 minutes if the coordinator takes 20 minutes to restart, or forever if the coordinator's log is lost, until an administrator steps in. Meanwhile other transactions that touch those rows are blocked, which can make large parts of an application unavailable; transactions on other rows are not blocked by it.

questions.question: What are orphaned in-doubt transactions in two-phase commit?

options.text: In-doubt transactions whose outcome the coordinator cannot determine, for example because its log was lost
Transactions that have no participants left, which are cleared automatically when the database is rebooted
Aborted transactions that were never cleaned up, which a background vacuum process removes in due course
Duplicate transactions created by client retries, which automatic deduplication on each participant resolves

questions.explanation: Orphaned in-doubt transactions are transactions for which the coordinator cannot decide the outcome, for instance because its transaction log was lost or corrupted by a software bug. They cannot be resolved automatically and sit in the database holding locks. Rebooting does not help, because a correct 2PC implementation must preserve an in-doubt transaction's locks across restarts to avoid breaking atomicity. An administrator must examine the participants and apply the same outcome to all of them.

questions.question: What is a heuristic decision in XA two-phase commit?

options.text: A participant unilaterally committing or aborting an in-doubt transaction, probably breaking atomicity
An optimization that skips the prepare phase in the common case, making two-phase commit faster overall
An automatic retry policy with exponential backoff that the coordinator uses for lost commit messages
A new coordinator election that the participants run among themselves after the coordinator crashes

questions.explanation: Many XA implementations offer heuristic decisions: a participant may unilaterally decide to commit or abort an in-doubt transaction without a definitive decision from the coordinator. 'Heuristic' is a euphemism for probably breaking atomicity, since it violates the system of promises that 2PC relies on. Heuristic decisions are intended only for escaping catastrophic situations, not for regular use.

questions.question: A key realization about XA transactions is that the transaction coordinator is itself a kind of database. Which consequences follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The coordinator's decision log must be treated with the same care as any important database
An unreplicated coordinator is a single point of failure for the entire system
A coordinator embedded in an application server makes that otherwise stateless server stateful
The coordinator must run inside every participant database to achieve acceptable latency

questions.explanation: Transaction outcomes are stored in the coordinator, so it needs database-grade care. If it is not replicated, its failure makes other application servers block on locks held by in-doubt transactions; surprisingly, many coordinators are not highly available by default. And when the coordinator lives in the application server, its logs become a crucial part of durable system state, so those servers are no longer stateless and cannot be added or removed at will.

optionExplanations.a: The coordinator's durable decision log is authoritative transaction state, so it needs database-grade replication, backup, and recovery. Treating it as disposable middleware can strand prepared participants.
optionExplanations.b: If an unreplicated coordinator and its log are lost, participants cannot learn whether to commit or abort. One coordinator failure can therefore block transactions across all participant systems.
optionExplanations.c: Stateless application servers can be added and removed freely because all persistent state is in the database. Embedding the coordinator's log in such a server makes its local disk crucial for recovering in-doubt transactions.
optionExplanations.d: The coordinator need not run inside each participant; XA deliberately coordinates separate resource managers from the application side. Co-location is neither a correctness requirement nor a latency fix.

questions.question: Why does XA behave as a lowest common denominator, and what can it therefore not do?

options.text: It must work with many data systems, so it cannot detect deadlocks across systems or work with SSI
It must avoid disk writes for portability, so it cannot keep a durable commit log on participants
It supports at most two participants per transaction, and it requires tightly synchronized clocks
It requires Byzantine fault tolerance from every participant, so it cannot be combined with replication

questions.explanation: Because XA has to work with a wide range of data systems, it supports only what they all have in common. Detecting deadlocks across systems would need a standard way of exchanging lock-wait information, and supporting SSI would need a protocol for identifying conflicts across systems; XA has neither. Database-internal distributed transactions are less limited (a distributed SSI is possible), but any 2PC still needs every participant to respond, so distributed transactions tend to amplify failures.

questions.question: How is the consensus problem normally formalized?

options.text: One or more nodes propose values, and the algorithm decides on one of those values
All nodes must propose the same value, and the algorithm confirms it
The algorithm invents a fresh value that no node proposed, so that no node's proposal is favoured
Each node decides independently, and the decisions are reconciled later

questions.explanation: Formally, one or more nodes may propose values and the consensus algorithm decides on one of them. For example, when several customers concurrently try to buy the last seat on a flight, each node handling a request may propose its customer's ID, and the decision says which customer gets the seat. Nodes may propose different values; the decided value must be one that was proposed, and all nodes must agree on it.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly state the properties a consensus algorithm must satisfy? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently
Integrity: no node decides twice
Validity: if a node decides value v, then v must have been proposed by a majority of nodes
Termination: every node that does not crash eventually decides some value

questions.explanation: Agreement prevents different decisions, integrity prevents a node from deciding twice, validity prevents fabricated values, and termination requires progress for nonfailed nodes. Safety covers the first three; termination is the liveness condition.

optionExplanations.a: Uniform agreement is the safety rule that no two nodes decide different values, including nodes that later crash. Without it the system would have split decisions rather than consensus.
optionExplanations.b: Integrity prevents a participant from changing its mind or deciding repeatedly. A decision is irrevocable, which lets later operations rely on it as stable shared state.
optionExplanations.c: Validity only requires a decided value to have been proposed by some participant, not by a majority. Majority support is an algorithmic technique, not part of the abstract validity property.
optionExplanations.d: Termination is the liveness condition that every noncrashed node eventually decides. It distinguishes a safe protocol that waits forever from one that actually makes progress under its assumptions.

questions.question: Which two consensus properties define its core idea, namely that everyone decides the same outcome and nobody changes their mind?

options.text: Uniform agreement and integrity
Validity and termination
Validity and integrity
Termination and uniform agreement

questions.explanation: Uniform agreement (no two nodes decide differently) and integrity (no node decides twice) together express the core of consensus. Validity (the decided value was proposed by some node) mainly rules out trivial solutions, such as an algorithm that always decides null, which would satisfy agreement and integrity but not validity. Termination is the liveness property that formalizes fault tolerance.

questions.question: What does the termination property of consensus formalize, and does two-phase commit satisfy it?

options.text: Fault tolerance: every node that does not crash must eventually decide; 2PC does not satisfy it
Safety: no two nodes may ever decide differently; 2PC satisfies it because the coordinator decides
Ordering: decisions must be made in timestamp order; 2PC satisfies it through its transaction IDs
Durability: decisions must survive crashes; 2PC does not need it because participants keep no logs

questions.explanation: Termination says a consensus algorithm cannot sit around doing nothing forever: even if some nodes fail, the others must still reach a decision. The consensus system model assumes a crashed node never comes back, so any algorithm that must wait for a node to recover cannot satisfy termination. 2PC is such an algorithm: in-doubt participants may wait forever for the coordinator. Termination is a liveness property, whereas agreement, integrity, and validity are safety properties.

questions.question: How many nodes must be functioning for a consensus algorithm to guarantee termination, and what happens to safety if more fail?

options.text: A majority; if more fail, progress stops but most implementations still never make an invalid decision
Just one; the single surviving node can then make every decision on its own, safely and without waiting
All of them; the failure of any single node immediately corrupts the decisions already made by the others
Two-thirds in the crash-fault case; with fewer, the remaining nodes may make conflicting decisions

questions.explanation: Any consensus algorithm needs at least a majority of nodes functioning correctly to assure termination; that majority can form a quorum. So termination assumes fewer than half the nodes are crashed or unreachable. Most implementations nevertheless guarantee the safety properties (agreement, integrity, validity) even if a majority fails or the network misbehaves badly: a large outage can stop progress but cannot corrupt the system into invalid decisions. The two-thirds threshold belongs to Byzantine tolerance.

questions.question: What fault model do most consensus algorithms assume?

options.text: Crash faults but no Byzantine faults: nodes may fail but follow the protocol honestly
Byzantine faults, tolerating up to half of all the nodes lying or behaving maliciously
Fault-free operation, so every node must stay up and connected throughout the protocol
Arbitrary faults affecting any number of the nodes at once, with no bound on their count
