questions.explanation: Most consensus algorithms assume there are no Byzantine faults: if a node does not follow the protocol correctly, for example by sending contradictory messages to different nodes, it may break the protocol's safety properties. Consensus can be made robust against Byzantine faults as long as fewer than one-third of the nodes are Byzantine-faulty, but that needs different algorithms. Tolerating crashes of a minority is the standard assumption.

questions.question: Which are the best-known fault-tolerant consensus algorithms?

options.text: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft, and Zab
Two-phase commit and three-phase commit
Gossip and anti-entropy dissemination protocols
Lamport timestamps and version vectors

questions.explanation: The best-known fault-tolerant consensus algorithms are Viewstamped Replication (VSR), Paxos, Raft, and Zab. They share many ideas but are not identical. Most decide a sequence of values rather than a single value, which makes them total order broadcast algorithms. Implementing one yourself is probably not advisable, because it is hard. 2PC is not fault-tolerant, gossip does not provide agreement, and timestamps are not consensus at all.

questions.question: Total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus, one decision per delivered message. Which correspondences between consensus properties and total order broadcast guarantees are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Agreement: all nodes decide to deliver the same messages in the same order
Integrity: messages are not duplicated
Validity: messages are not corrupted and not fabricated out of thin air
Termination: every message is delivered within a bounded time after being sent

questions.explanation: Each round of consensus decides the next message to deliver. Agreement makes all nodes deliver the same messages in the same order, integrity means messages are not duplicated, validity means messages are not corrupted or fabricated, and termination means messages are not lost. Termination gives eventual delivery, not a time bound. VSR, Raft, and Zab implement total order broadcast directly because it is more efficient than repeated one-value consensus; for Paxos this optimization is called Multi-Paxos.

optionExplanations.a: Consensus agreement yields identical delivery sequences at every node: each log position is the same decision everywhere. Different message order would imply different decisions.
optionExplanations.b: Consensus integrity makes each log-position decision irrevocable and nonrepeating, which corresponds to a message not being delivered twice at one node.
optionExplanations.c: Validity prevents the protocol from inventing or corrupting a proposed value. For broadcast, delivered messages must be messages that were actually sent.
optionExplanations.d: Termination promises eventual delivery under the model's progress assumptions, not a fixed time bound. Asynchronous networks can delay a correct delivery arbitrarily long.

questions.question: When human operators manually choose and configure a new leader after the old one fails, how does this compare with consensus?

options.text: A dictatorial form of consensus that works in practice but lacks termination, since progress needs humans
It satisfies every consensus property, including termination, because operators always eventually act
It avoids the need for any agreement about who the leader is, since only one human makes the choice
It is equivalent to automatic failover with a proven consensus algorithm, just with slower reaction times

questions.explanation: If humans pick and configure the leader, only that node may decide the order of writes, a 'consensus algorithm' of the dictatorial variety. If the leader goes down, the system is unavailable for writes until operators configure another one. Such a system can work well in practice, but it does not satisfy termination, because progress depends on human action. Automatic leader election moves closer to fault-tolerant total order broadcast but needs real consensus to avoid split brain.

questions.question: Consensus protocols internally use a leader. What guarantee do they make about leader uniqueness?

options.text: A unique leader within each epoch (ballot, view, or term), not at all times
A unique leader at all times, identified by the sequence number of its latest log entry
Leaderless rounds in which every node proposes values independently
A unique leader per data partition, fixed when the cluster is first configured

questions.explanation: Consensus protocols do not guarantee a unique leader at every moment. Instead they define an epoch number, called the ballot number in Paxos, the view number in Viewstamped Replication, and the term number in Raft, and guarantee that within each epoch the leader is unique. Two leaders from different epochs may briefly coexist, and the one with the higher epoch prevails. Leadership is not fixed at configuration time; a new epoch and election start whenever the current leader is thought to be dead.

questions.question: How are epoch numbers assigned in consensus protocols, and which leader prevails in a conflict?

options.text: Each election gets an incremented epoch number; the leader with the higher epoch prevails
Epoch numbers are chosen at random by each candidate; the leader with the lower number prevails
Epoch numbers come from wall-clock time; the leader with the later clock prevails
Epoch numbers never change; the first leader ever elected always prevails

questions.explanation: Whenever the current leader is thought to be dead, the nodes start a vote to elect a new leader, and that election gets an incremented epoch number. Epoch numbers are therefore totally ordered and monotonically increasing. If two leaders from different epochs conflict, perhaps because the previous leader was not actually dead, the leader with the higher epoch prevails. Wall-clock time is not used, because clocks are unreliable.

questions.question: Before a consensus leader decides anything, how does it confirm that it has not been ousted by a leader with a higher epoch?

options.text: It sends the proposal to the other nodes and waits for a quorum to vote for it; nodes refuse if aware of a higher epoch
It checks its own local state, since a node can always trust its own belief that it is currently the leader of the cluster
It compares its physical clock with the clocks of the other nodes, and continues only if its own clock is the most recent
It waits for a fixed timeout, and assumes it is still leader if no other node contacts it meanwhile

questions.explanation: A node cannot trust its own judgment: believing it is leader does not mean the others accept it. So for every decision, the leader sends the proposed value to the other nodes and waits for a quorum (typically a majority) to respond in favor. A node votes for a proposal only if it is not aware of any leader with a higher epoch. The truth is defined by the majority, not by the node's own belief or its clock.

questions.question: Consensus protocols hold one vote to elect a leader and another to accept each of the leader's proposals. Why does this keep decisions safe?

options.text: The two quorums must overlap, so a successful proposal vote includes a node that knows of any newer election
The two quorums must be disjoint, so that no single node can bias the outcome by voting in both of the rounds
Only one vote is really needed for safety, and the second vote exists purely as an optimization for performance
Both votes must be unanimous, so that every node in the cluster always agrees on every decision that is made

questions.explanation: The key insight is that the quorum for the election and the quorum for each proposal must overlap: if a proposal vote succeeds, at least one of the voting nodes also took part in the most recent leader election. So if no voter reports a higher epoch, the leader can conclude no newer election has happened and safely decide the value. With majority quorums, any two majorities intersect; unanimity is not required.

questions.question: Epoch-based voting in consensus algorithms looks superficially like two-phase commit. Which of the following are real differences? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In 2PC the coordinator is not elected
Consensus needs votes from only a majority, whereas 2PC needs a yes from every participant
Consensus defines a recovery process that brings nodes to a consistent state after a new leader is elected
2PC relies on epoch numbers, whereas consensus algorithms manage without them

questions.explanation: The biggest differences are that the 2PC coordinator is not elected, that fault-tolerant consensus needs only a majority of votes whereas 2PC needs a yes from every participant, and that consensus algorithms define a recovery process ensuring the safety properties hold after a leader change. These differences are what make consensus correct and fault-tolerant where 2PC blocks. Epoch numbers belong to consensus, not 2PC.

optionExplanations.a: In two-phase commit the coordinator is fixed in advance, typically by the application, and is not chosen by a fault-tolerant election. Consensus elects leaders through numbered epochs.
optionExplanations.b: Consensus can decide with a majority because intersecting majorities preserve earlier decisions despite minority failures. 2PC needs every participant's yes because each owns part of the transaction.
optionExplanations.c: After a leader change, a consensus protocol reconciles nodes so the new leader preserves every decision already made. Plain 2PC instead leaves prepared participants waiting for the old coordinator.
optionExplanations.d: Epoch numbers are a consensus mechanism for distinguishing successive leaders. Standard two-phase commit has no elected leaders and therefore no epochs, so the statement is reversed.

questions.question: What do consensus algorithms provide that makes them a breakthrough for distributed systems?

options.text: Safety properties (agreement, integrity, validity) while staying fault-tolerant as long as a majority works
Eventual consistency without any majority requirement, so even one surviving node can keep making decisions
Tolerance of one node failure with a cluster of only two nodes, halving the hardware needed for replication
Fully asynchronous operation with no replication cost at all, since nodes never have to wait for each other

questions.explanation: Consensus brings concrete safety properties to systems where everything else is uncertain, and remains able to make progress as long as a majority of nodes are working and reachable. Because consensus provides total order broadcast, it can also implement linearizable atomic operations fault-tolerantly. The benefits have costs: voting is a kind of synchronous replication, and tolerating one failure needs at least three nodes.

questions.question: Besides the cost of synchronous voting and the need for a strict majority, which further limitations do consensus algorithms have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Static membership complicates adding or removing voting nodes
Variable delay causes false suspicions and disruptive leader elections
One unreliable link can cause pathological leadership churn
Any merely slow node is Byzantine and immediately violates safety

questions.explanation: Most consensus algorithms assume a fixed set of voting nodes, and dynamic membership extensions are much less well understood. They rely on timeouts, so variable network delays can trigger false suspicions and frequent leader elections that hurt performance without harming safety. Some, such as Raft, have unpleasant edge cases where one consistently unreliable link makes leadership bounce between nodes. Designing algorithms more robust to unreliable networks was still an open research problem at the time of writing.

optionExplanations.a: Changing the voting membership safely is itself a coordinated transition because old and new quorums must overlap appropriately. Static configurations avoid that complexity but hinder elasticity.
optionExplanations.b: Timeouts cannot distinguish a failed leader from a delayed one, so variable latency can trigger unnecessary elections. Safety remains intact, but availability and throughput may collapse.
optionExplanations.c: A repeatedly unreliable link can make one node alternate between reachable and suspected, causing leadership churn. Some protocols need additional defenses against this pathological pattern.
optionExplanations.d: A slow node is a crash-suspicion problem, not automatically Byzantine. Consensus safety is designed to survive delay; Byzantine behavior means arbitrary or malicious protocol violations.

questions.question: How are projects like ZooKeeper and etcd usually described?

options.text: As distributed key-value stores, or as coordination and configuration services
As high-throughput message brokers for streaming large volumes of events to consumers
As relational databases offering full SQL queries and multi-table joins
As in-memory caches that evict the least recently used keys when they fill up

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper and etcd are usually described as distributed key-value stores or coordination and configuration services, and their API looks much like a database's: read and write a key's value and iterate over keys. Yet they go to the effort of implementing consensus because of what they are used for. Application developers rarely use ZooKeeper directly; more often they rely on it indirectly through projects such as HBase, Hadoop YARN, OpenStack Nova, and Kafka.

questions.question: What amount of data are ZooKeeper and etcd designed to hold, and how is it replicated?

options.text: Small amounts fitting in memory (also written to disk), replicated to all nodes by total order broadcast
Terabytes of data stored on disk, replicated across nodes using sloppy quorum writes with hinted handoff
Data held only in memory with no durability, so a restart of every node loses all of the stored state
Arbitrary amounts of application data, replicated asynchronously from a single leader to its followers

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper and etcd hold small amounts of data that can fit entirely in memory, though they still write it to disk for durability; you would not store all your application's data there. That data is replicated across all nodes using a fault-tolerant total order broadcast algorithm, and applying the same writes in the same order keeps the replicas consistent.

questions.question: In a coordination service like ZooKeeper, which primitive lets you implement a lock, and how is the lock usually made safe against a client failing while holding it?

options.text: A linearizable atomic compare-and-set; the lock is usually a lease with an expiry time
A plain read-write register; the lock is held forever until explicitly released
A timestamp comparison; the lock relies on tightly synchronized clocks to expire on time
A quorum read; the lock is released automatically when the network partition heals

questions.explanation: With an atomic compare-and-set, only one of several nodes concurrently trying the same operation succeeds, which is exactly a lock. The consensus protocol makes the operation atomic and linearizable even if a node fails or the network is interrupted. A distributed lock is usually implemented as a lease with an expiry time, so that it is eventually released if the client fails.

questions.question: A lock is implemented as a lease. The client holding it pauses, the lease expires, and another client acquires the lock. What prevents the paused client from corrupting the protected resource when it resumes, and how does ZooKeeper provide it?

options.text: A fencing token that increases on each acquisition; ZooKeeper's zxid or version number can serve
A cryptographic nonce that prevents replay; ZooKeeper generates a fresh random nonce for every lock
The client's session ID, which ZooKeeper reuses unchanged on each acquisition of the same lock
The lease itself, because once it expires the old holder is guaranteed to stop acting immediately

questions.explanation: A fencing token is a number that increases every time the lock is acquired; the protected resource rejects requests carrying a token older than one it has already seen, so the resumed client's stale requests are refused. ZooKeeper provides such numbers by totally ordering all operations and giving each a monotonically increasing transaction ID (zxid) and version number (cversion). A lease alone is not enough, because a paused client may not realize it has expired.

questions.question: How does ZooKeeper detect that a client has failed?

options.text: Sessions with periodic heartbeats; if heartbeats stop beyond the session timeout, the session is declared dead
Clients poll the server on every operation, and ZooKeeper keeps no concept of a session for any client
The server pings each client once per hour, and locks held by a failed client are never released automatically
Any brief connection interruption immediately ends the session and releases every lock it was holding

questions.explanation: Clients maintain a long-lived session on the ZooKeeper servers, and client and server periodically exchange heartbeats. Even if the connection is temporarily interrupted or a ZooKeeper node fails, the session remains active; only if heartbeats cease for longer than the session timeout is the session declared dead. Locks held by a session can be configured to be released automatically when it times out; ZooKeeper calls these ephemeral nodes.

questions.question: Besides reading values, what does ZooKeeper let a client do with locks and values created by other clients?

options.text: Watch them for changes and be notified, for example when a client joins or its ephemeral nodes vanish
Only poll them repeatedly, since ZooKeeper offers no change notifications for keys created by others
Subscribe to changes, but only on keys that the subscribing client itself created at some earlier point
Receive notifications about other clients' keys, but only at the moment its own session finally ends

questions.explanation: A client can watch keys for changes, so it can learn when another client joins the cluster (based on a value it writes) or fails (because its session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear), without frequent polling. Of ZooKeeper's features (linearizable atomic operations, total ordering, failure detection, change notifications), only the linearizable atomic operations truly require consensus, but the combination is what makes it so useful for coordination.

questions.question: In which kinds of tasks does the ZooKeeper (or Chubby) coordination model work well? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Electing a leader or primary and failing it over
Assigning resource partitions to nodes
Rebalancing partitions as cluster membership changes
Storing the application's large primary dataset directly

questions.explanation: Coordination services suit tasks such as choosing a leader or primary among several instances of a service (and failing over when it dies), and assigning partitions of a resource such as a database, message streams, or file storage to nodes, rebalancing as nodes join, leave, or fail. Atomic operations, ephemeral nodes, and change notifications let applications do this and recover from faults automatically. It is not easy even with libraries such as Apache Curator, but it beats implementing consensus from scratch. ZooKeeper is not designed to store an application's large primary dataset.

optionExplanations.a: Ephemeral nodes, atomic creation, and watches let contenders agree on one current leader and notice its session failure. Applications avoid implementing election and failover consensus themselves.
optionExplanations.b: Coordination metadata can assign each resource partition to exactly one worker. Watches then notify workers when ownership changes so processing can follow the agreed assignment.
optionExplanations.c: Membership changes can trigger a coordinated reassignment recorded in ZooKeeper or Chubby. The service supplies the small, strongly consistent state needed to rebalance safely.
optionExplanations.d: Coordination services are optimized for small, slowly changing metadata, not high-volume application records. Using one as the primary data store would create a throughput and capacity bottleneck.

questions.question: An application grows from running on one node to running on thousands of nodes. How does ZooKeeper handle coordination for that many nodes?

options.text: It runs on a small fixed set of nodes (usually three or five) that vote among themselves while serving many clients
It adds every new application node to its voting set, so that majority votes always include the whole application
It refuses connections beyond a hard limit of about 100 clients, so large applications must shard their coordination
It requires each application node to run its own independent ZooKeeper instance, so that voting stays purely local

questions.explanation: Majority votes across thousands of nodes would be terribly inefficient. Instead ZooKeeper runs on a fixed small number of nodes, usually three or five, and performs majority votes among them while supporting a potentially large number of clients. This lets applications outsource coordination work (consensus, operation ordering, and failure detection) to an external service. Independent ZooKeeper instances per node would not agree with each other.

questions.question: What kind of data belongs in ZooKeeper, and what does not?

options.text: Slow-changing coordination data, such as which node leads partition 7, but not fast-changing runtime state
Fast-changing runtime application state, but not slow-changing coordination metadata such as partition leaders
Both kinds of data, since its replicated log handles any rate of change and any data volume equally well
Bulk application records and user data, but not leadership or cluster membership information about nodes

questions.explanation: Data managed by ZooKeeper is normally slow-changing, such as 'the node running on 10.1.1.23 is the leader for partition 7', which may change on a timescale of minutes or hours. It is not intended for the application's runtime state, which may change thousands or millions of times per second. If such state must be replicated, other tools such as Apache BookKeeper can be used.

questions.question: Does service discovery (finding which IP address to connect to for a given service) require consensus?

options.text: Not necessarily: like DNS lookups, it can usually tolerate slightly stale, non-linearizable reads
Yes: service discovery strictly requires linearizable reads, so it can only be built on a consensus system
No, and for the same reason leader election does not require consensus either
Yes, because every IP address in the service registry must be unique, which is a uniqueness constraint

questions.explanation: It is less clear that service discovery needs consensus. DNS, the traditional way to look up a service's address, uses layers of caching, its reads are not linearizable, and slightly stale results are usually fine; availability matters more. Leader election does need consensus, so if a consensus system already knows the leader, it can help others discover it. Some consensus systems support read-only caching replicas that asynchronously receive the log of decisions without voting and serve reads that need not be linearizable.

questions.question: What does a membership service determine, and why is it useful even though failure detection is unreliable?

options.text: Which nodes are live members; combining failure detection with consensus gives every node the same view
Which nodes are live members, detected perfectly by timeouts so that no live node is ever declared dead
Which nodes are live members, determined by gossip so that each node keeps its own independent opinion
Which nodes are live members, determined by comparing the synchronized physical clocks of all the nodes

questions.explanation: A membership service determines which nodes are currently active members of a cluster. Because of unbounded network delays, failures cannot be detected reliably, but coupling failure detection with consensus lets nodes agree on which nodes are alive. A node may still be wrongly declared dead, but agreement is valuable: for example, choosing the lowest-numbered member as leader only works if all nodes have the same view of the membership. Such services go back to research in the 1980s, used for example in air traffic control.

questions.question: A wide range of problems are equivalent to consensus, meaning a solution to one can be transformed into a solution to the others. Which of the following are among them? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Linearizable compare-and-set registers, and atomic commit of distributed transactions
Total order broadcast of messages to all nodes in one agreed delivery order
Locks and leases, and membership or coordination services built on failure detectors
Detecting concurrent writes to one key with version vectors, as leaderless stores do

questions.explanation: Each equivalent problem requires an irrevocable decision that all nodes agree on: a compare-and-set register decides whether to set its value, atomic commit decides commit or abort, total order broadcast decides the delivery order, a lock decides which client acquired it, and a membership service decides which nodes are alive. (Uniqueness constraints belong to the same family.) Detecting concurrent writes with version vectors makes no such decision: it only records that two writes are concurrent and leaves both siblings for later merging, so it works without coordination and is not equivalent to consensus.

optionExplanations.a: A linearizable compare-and-set must decide atomically whether to set its value, and atomic commit must decide one outcome for all participants. Both are irrevocable shared decisions reducible to consensus.
optionExplanations.b: Total order broadcast repeatedly decides the next message in one common sequence. Consensus can build that sequence, and the sequence can in turn implement consensus.
optionExplanations.c: When clients race for a lock or lease, the lock decides which one acquired it; a membership service decides which nodes count as alive given a failure detector. Both require agreed, irrevocable decisions.
optionExplanations.d: Version vectors only detect that two writes are concurrent and keep both as siblings; nobody has to pick a winner, so leaderless stores do this without any coordination. That is why it is not equivalent to consensus.

questions.question: Problems such as compare-and-set, atomic commit, total order broadcast, locks, membership, and uniqueness constraints are all equivalent to consensus. When are they straightforward to solve?

options.text: With one node, or with every decision assigned to one node, as in a single-leader database
When a majority of the nodes agree among themselves, without any leader being needed for it
When all of the nodes' physical clocks are synchronized to within a single millisecond
When every node decides on its own using only its local state, without contacting others

questions.explanation: All of these are straightforward on a single node, or if you are willing to give all decision-making power to a single node. That is what a single-leader database does, which is why it can provide linearizable operations, uniqueness constraints, and a totally ordered replication log. The difficulty appears when that single leader fails or becomes unreachable. Majority agreement without a leader is itself the consensus problem, and independent local decisions would disagree.

questions.question: When the single leader of a system fails or becomes unreachable, which ways of handling the situation exist, and what are their drawbacks? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Wait for the old leader, which may block forever
Use manual failover, which is slow human consensus
Elect a new leader automatically with a proven consensus protocol
Permit concurrent leaders and rely on conflict resolution for consensus

questions.explanation: Waiting for the old leader to recover preserves safety but may block forever if it never returns; many XA/JTA transaction coordinators work this way. Manual failover has humans choose and configure a new leader, a kind of consensus by 'act of God' that is limited by how fast people can act. Electing a new leader automatically requires a consensus algorithm, ideally a proven one that handles adverse network conditions, and it is the only approach that keeps making progress through leader failure without human help. Letting concurrent leaders run is split brain, not a way of handling leader failure.

optionExplanations.a: Waiting avoids two leaders and therefore preserves safety, but a permanently failed leader means the system may never resume. It sacrifices liveness rather than solving failover.
optionExplanations.b: An operator can gather evidence and designate a replacement, effectively performing slow consensus outside the protocol. Safety depends on human coordination and recovery time is unpredictable.
optionExplanations.c: A proven consensus protocol elects one replacement through quorum agreement and numbered epochs. This supplies automatic progress while fencing leaders from older epochs.
optionExplanations.d: Allowing concurrent leaders abandons the single agreed leadership decision. Conflict resolution may merge ordinary data later, but it cannot make both leaders' exclusive actions safe.

questions.question: A single-leader database provides linearizability without running a consensus algorithm on every write. Why does it still require consensus?

options.text: It needs consensus to keep its leadership and to change leaders safely
It needs consensus so followers can agree on how far each has replicated the log
It needs consensus to give each client a consistent choice of replica to read from
It needs consensus for its reads, but never for choosing a leader

questions.explanation: A single leader makes everyday decisions alone, but deciding who the leader is, and changing leaders when one fails, still requires consensus to avoid split brain. In that sense having a leader only 'kicks the can down the road': consensus is still needed, just in a different place and less often. Followers simply apply the leader's log in order, and routing clients to replicas needs no agreement, so neither requires consensus. Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms and systems exist for exactly this purpose.

questions.question: What role do tools like ZooKeeper play for applications?

options.text: An outsourced consensus, failure detection, and membership service
A general-purpose database that replaces relational systems
A message broker for high-throughput event streams
A reference design that each application should reimplement itself

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper provides consensus, failure detection, and membership as an outsourced service that applications can use. It is not easy to use, but it is much better than developing your own algorithms that must withstand all the problems of distributed systems. If you need something reducible to consensus and want it fault-tolerant, using such a tool is advisable. It is not designed for general-purpose data storage or high-throughput streaming.
